Heading: Luxury Lineup - Indian Express
Content:
Swaran Singh discusses the repercussions of partition in India Encircled

The freedom struggle of a country is always a landmark that is talked about for ages. In India itself it is alive, on celluloid, in people's mind and in the written word. Adding yet another thought to the same is Sangram Singh with his book India Encircled, and the similarities with his name is not only reason that he is attached to the issue. "Those times have been our recent past, in a way the embers have still not died. So in my first book I have talked about what I have found out through my research," he tells. And we get to read his opinion on how partition could have been avoided and how leaders like Nehru failed in handling the partition, "due to their half-hearted attempts."

"Some historians opine that coming of the Mughals put the clock back on India's modernization. This is far from the truth. It was actually the Europeans who copied our methods of agriculture and industry. After gaining territorial control they also sowed seeds of dissension in our people, " the book goes on to tell. There are twelve chapters that discuss issues like Communal Divide, Reservation on Caste Basis, Scams, Views of RSS Ideologues, Views of Ullemahs, Healing Touch for Kashmiri Pandits and Appeal to His Holiness the Pope.

"Till date we are facing the repercussions, the governments have failed to take care of what followed. I hope the future holds better," he signs off.

Heading: The man behind the camera - Indian Express
Content:
From Indian designers Rohit Bal to Raghavendra Rathore, Ashish Soni to Malini Ramani to international biggies like Valentino, Poleci and even Christies, they are all hitting the city today!

OK, while we do know that this city of ours is hip, happening and all big brands love us but this comes a tad unexpected. At a time when the big, glitzy metros are raising toasts to Fashion Weeks, back home this is nothing short of a designer frenzy. In fact the invites arrived back to back. Come Tuesday, October 7 and Chandigarh will see not just leading Indian designer wear up for grabs but a chance for the city's fashionistas to get a feel of international biggies. Here's the who, what and where of it all.

A trunk show : If you like the way the swish set dress up in Europe, here's your chance to look the same. The ladies can drool over bags that the likes of Catherine Zeta Jones and Lindsay Lohan swear by. For coming in at the Taj on Tuesday will be the iconic American luxury handbag brand Judith Leiber along with international brands such as Poleci, Christies and Argentovivo as part of a one-day trunk show. Bringing them in is Sangeeta Assomull of the Marigold group. "I have heard so much about Chandigarh, its well-heeled fashionable crowd that we feel it's time we brought a trunk show like this," remarked Sangeeta who finds it a unique way to introduce people to global fashion. So what can one lay hands on? "Apart from a stunning collection of evening clutch bags in crystal by Judith Leiber, there will be Poleci's collection in luxurious satins and lurex along with statement pieces in silver grey along with detailed sequin halter neck tops and sheer chiffon blouses, complimented by beautifully tailored skirts and trousers," she says. Also on the racks will be formal and evening wear by Italian biggie Christies and a lingerie line by Argentovivo as well as Les Copains' most recent Autumn/Winter 2008 collection. A nose for fashion apart, make sure you carry a fat wallet along!

Take the fiest row : With a name that says it all, First Row, a Mumbai-based outfit spearheaded by Radhika Dhawan and Nupur Mendiratta, promises to get you access to collections of some of the leading designers in the country. "Till now one had to head to the big cities to lay one's hands on labels by Ashish Soni or Gaurav Gupta or Gauri & Nainika or even Rohit Bal. Instead with this show we are bringing the designers to your doorstep, quite literally," explains Radhika who finds that even designers want to tap unexplored markets. Well, with their first show the two chose Chandigarh. "It's a discerning market with tastes for the best," tells Radhika who also brings with her Raghavendra Rathore, Rohit Bal, Shantanu & Nikhil and Valentino. The range on offer will include collections for men and women, Western to Indian wear, and also accessories. "There will be a selection of sarees, lehengas, salwar suits, dresses, menswear, shoes, bags and all over cookies and coffee and at special prices," smiles Dhawan who will put up the show on Tuesday and Wednesday at Hotel Mountview.

Heading: Finally, Army hands over Gobindgarh Fort to admn - Indian Express
Content:
In Raghu Rai's world, creativity is all about capturing the mystery of things, and photography, a yogic exercise that centres on energy

Must a picture tell a story… must it speak a thousand words? For all those who live by clichés, conditioned to follow programmed lives, a picture reduces to a mad man's abstract piece of art lest it fails to evoke an essay of words. On the other hand, clichés are of no consequence in Padamshree Raghu Rai's world. "A thousand words can be a lot of noise," says the famed photographer during an interaction at the Government Museum and Art Gallery courtesy the Lalit Kala Academy.

"A guru restores the silence in you. A great piece of art does the same, and in its silence, lie answers. The work fulfills you, there are no more questions to be asked." The silence reflects as the computer throws a slideshow of his photographs on the wall, filling up the white space. "Black and white photographs always silence the noise of colour while colour has to blend well to say something," feels Rai, humouring how he has come to 'uproot' us. "Settlement is boring, repetitive existence where we tend to lose a sense of exploration," something which Rai has never let go, his appetite for more. In his interaction, Rai, unconsciously perhaps, opened windows to his life. Artist, poet, philosopher, Rai reflected many facets to him, the greatest being his humility, his sense of humour, his eagerness to live a million lives in one, a childlike enthusiasm to discover new forms and concepts, to capture the energies and wrap himself in them… "each time I put the camera on my eye and look, my energies get concentrated and I start looking closely at the world. Before I know, it transforms into a yogic exercise for me." For Raghu, art is not about beauty. "It's first about capturing human expression, energy, intensity, the magic of it all, and then beauty follows. But first, you make a connection." What were the prints of a programmed mind in his earlier works have now transitioned into magical moments. "Touch and go, that's what creativity is, a soft whisper. I have come to realize that when you make yourself available wholly, then nature helps you get what you want," Rai clicks on the pictures which were 'godsend magical gifts'. Mother Teresa in deep prayer, Indira Gandhi in deep thought, musicians in a rapture, pundits in awe at Akshardham, a baby's burial post Bhopal gas tragedy, Calcutta's blue docks, purani Dilli, old bazaars of India.

He doesn't believe in 'nostalgic nonsense' for he believes he is still interacting with life, living in the present. His idea of infotainment is again nonsensical - "It's all Bollywood kachra and same dirty politics catering to urban India. " Perhaps this is the reason Rai never took up fashion photography, "branded middle class mediocrity" he calls it. Perhaps this is also the reason he's been documenting a lot of works including his own in the form of books, "for history can be written and rewritten, but you can never re-write photo history. " These days Rai's just finished editing a book on Delhi and is already on to his next, on Indian classical musicians. And yes, wherever his travels take him, he brings home that part of the world with him, "and plant it in my home."

When it comes to capturing the world, India is more than enough says Rai. "The experience of India is multi-layered and it's never one moment in space." Like and electric current, the images flow through him, capturing the essence to the last detail.

Heading: Security grounded, smugglers fly high - Indian Express
Content:
Govt plans to use fort as national museum to promote tourism

After a wait of more than 150 years, the Army today handed over the historic Gobindgarh Fort, which had been in its possession since 1849, to the civic administration.

The decision, which was taken after several meetings between the bureaucracy, Army and political leaders, has brought cheers among the people who had been waiting to have an access to the legacy of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

The government now plans to use the fort as a national museum to promote tourism in the state. Earlier, Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh had handed over the keys of the fort to the then chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh in 2006, but it had still remained inaccessible to the people. Today, Maj-Gen PS Paul, General Officer Commanding, Panther Division, handed over the control to Deputy Commissioner K S Pannu.

Addressing a gathering, Maj-Gen Paul said the fort, built in 1760, was named after Guru Gobind Singh by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and occupied a place of pride in the Indian history. He added that the Army had done its best to preserve the legacy of Maharaja Ranjit Singh with whatever resources were available with them.

"The fort was initially known as 'Bhangian Da Qila' as bhangis were one of the 12 Sikh misls," he said.

Pannu said the fort came under the control of the Army in 1849, when the British annexed Punjab after Maharaja Ranjit Singh's death. "However, the Indian Army took over it in 1948 and 26 units had been stationed here since then," the DC said. He added that an understanding has been reached with the Army, which would still hold a part of the fort. "This part has been properly segregated with the help of a wall, and a special road has been constructed to provide a separate entry," he said.

The DC said the government was now faced with the monumental task of conservation and generation of funds for the upkeep of the fort. He said some of the landmarks inside the fort that need immediate attention include bungalow of General O' Dyer and the Durbar Hall. Its important attractions include the 'toshkhana' or the treasury that was also used for storing provisions for the Maharaja's army, Nalwa Gate and the Keelar Gate.

Fort may hit silver screen, says DC

Claiming that Bollywood has evinced keen interest in Amritsar, DC K S Pannu today said the historic fort was likely to be featured in movies and serials. "Being associated with the legacy of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who has always attracted filmmakers, the place is historically and architecturally important, which is why we are expecting that it may feature in several movies soon," he said.

Heading: Girl alleges classmates assaulted her - Indian Express
Content:
Rajasansi Airport emerging as major transit route for drugs to Canada; about 26 kgs recovered in last six months

Rajasansi International Airport is fast gaining the dubious distinction of a transit point for drugs to Western countries, especially Canada.

In the last six months, over 26 kilograms of heroin has been recovered from NRIs, who were trying to ferry it to Canada, where the drug is in high demand.

The border town of Amritsar is a transit point in the drugs' trade route, which originates from Afghanistan. The narcotics smuggled from Pakistan find their way to Indian metros, also through the city.

Ever since the international flights started operating from here three years ago, the smugglers have made good use of the laxity of law enforcement agencies.

Yesterday's incident in which an NRI couple, Raminder Singh Nagra and Harjinder Kaur Nagram, was nabbed by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) with 3.7 kilograms of heroin is not an isolated case. The DRI had nabbed a Youth SAD leader, hailing from Jalandhar, with 23 kilograms of heroin six months ago, when he was about to board the Amritsar-Birmingham-Toronto flight.

In 2006, the DRI nabbed another NRI, who was trying to smuggle 7 kilograms of heroin to Canada through the same flight.

"Canada is emerging as a major market for drugs. From there, narcotics also enter the US. Due to bumper crop of opium in Afghanistan and its easy availability, smugglers have become very active and are using every possible way to mint money," said an intelligence official.

BS Sra, Chief Commissioner of the Customs Department, which has come under fire, admitted that twice the smugglers called the bluff of their staff.

"Though we are always vigilant, but I do not deny some laxity on part of our employees who cleared the luggage yesterday," he said, while not ruling out action against the guilty. "We will take extra precaution now," Sra added.

It was the DRI team, led by Ramesh Sharma, that promptly deplaned the couple and nabbed them minutes before the flight was to take off.

Though the security is tight at the airport, the staff is less in number, ill-equipped and even ill-trained to detect drugs.

"There are three x-ray machines to check luggage, but only two are in working condition. Besides, employees are not trained to spot the camouflaged drugs," said sources.

Meanwhile, the DRI today released Harjinder Kaur, saying that she was not involved in drug trade, and took Raminder Singh on a three-day remand.

Dog squad must

A sniffer dogs' squad is a must at the airport. Customs officials and Airport Director Arun Talwar claimed that they have requested the government for the squad, and would get it soon.

Heading: Man acquitted after 18 years - Indian Express
Content:
A girl student of Apeejay School filed a police complaint against her four classmates of class XII (non-medical stream) for beating her up on the school premises in the presence of the school authorities.

SHO of police division 4 Nirmal Singh said Heena, in her complaint to the police, said today when she went to the school, a group of four to five girls attacked her, while the school authorities remained a mute spectator.

"When the principal did not heed to her complaint, I took her to the Civil Hospital for medical examination," said Heena's mother Dr Nisha, adding that 15 days ago, same girls had fought with her daughter at a party.

"Following the incident, I didn't send Heena to school for about 15 days, as she was under stress. And today when she went to the school, they thrashed her and kicked her in the stomach," alleged the mother.

The SHO said a DDR has been registered and the parents of all the students would be called for a patch up.

Principal of the school Ranjna Sood said as she was not aware of the police complaint, she would not like to comment on it.

Heading: Eyes will be sent for DNA test - Indian Express
Content: Eighteen years after a man was booked for dacoity in a dera, a designated TADA court on Monday acquitted him for want of evidence. Mahinder Singh Titu was produced before the designate TADA court of Additional Sessions Judge Buaji Sansi, who after listening to the arguments of both the defence and the prosecution, ordered his acquittal due to lack of evidence. Other six accused in the case have already been acquitted.

Heading: In Mansa, man killed over Rs 100 - Indian Express
Content:
A team of experts at Patiala Medical College and Hospital today examined the eyes recovered from the accused in the eye scam, and said that they were of humans.

Meanwhile, the cops have also recovered the knife used by the accused, Sunil, to take out the eyes from the bodies at Ambala Civil Hospital.

Patiala SP (D) GS Chauhan told The Indian Express that the eyes examined by the experts' panel would be sent to Chandigarh for DNA test. "We will take DNA samples of the deceased's family member to match them," he added.

Senior police officials said they would get important leads in the case only after the arrest of Dr Neelima Sodhi, a co-accused.

"Phone records show the nexus between all the accused, as the number of calls was more on days the eyes were to be collected," they said.

Rajpura CIA in-charge SS Cheema said crucial records at Aggarsain Hospital have not been maintained and the entry registers had no record of any visiting faculty member.

Sources in the Police Department said the accused were visiting doctors at Aggarsain Hospital that charged a fixed amount for every operation and took no other responsibility towards the patients. "Interestingly, a nurse who joined the hospital a year back, when Dr Neelima also joined the hospital, had earlier worked with an eye specialist who was once arrested in another eye scam, but was later released by the court," they said. "Sunil, an employee of Government Hospital, Ambala, used to deliver the bodies to the relatives after the post-mortem. He used to inform another accused, Manjit Verma, driver of the doctor couple who would come to Ambala and pay Rs 1,500 for a pair of eyes that Sunil provided him," reads the FIR.

Heading: Terror’s ‘control room’ - Indian Express
Content:
This is the pits. A man was killed following a dispute over Rs 100 in a Mansa village past midnight today.

Ajaib Singh allegedly attacked Harmail Singh, alias Mela, an employee of the Punjab State Electricity Board (PSEB), with an axe at 1 am while he was sleeping in his house in Bahadurpur village. They had been locked in a dispute over Rs 100 for the past few days.

Police have arrested Ajaib Singh and recovered the axe used in the crime. "Ajaib has confessed to have murdered Harmail by hitting him with the blunt side of the axe," said Mansa SSP Manminder Singh.

Bareta SHO Major Singh said by the time deceased's wife, who was sleeping nearby with two kids, raised the alarm after hearing her husband's cries, the accused had escaped by jumping the not-so-high wall of the house.

Mela, who had three tractors, used to level the land by filling earth. Ajaib hired his service for getting his few acres levelled, for which Mela was promised a wage of Rs 1,000. But Ajaib charged Mela with not turning up for the work on time and not doing it properly, and paid him Rs 900.

Mela insisted on getting the remaining amount of Rs 100, which led to bad blood between the two. "A few days back, Mela intercepted Ajaib and forcibly took Rs 100 from his pocket, and thrashed him," said DSP (D) Jaspal Singh.

He said Ajaib murdered Harmail to take revenge for the humiliation. The DSP said Ajaib was from a village in Sunam, and claimed before the police that he was acquitted in a murder case earlier.

Heading: GIS plan misses date with Games - Indian Express
Content:
Eight IM men arrested; explosives sent not only to Surat but Pune too

Pune, often described as the country's cultural and educational capital, received a jolt to its image with the revelation that the Indian Mujahideen (IM) was using the city as its "control room" and a hub for jihadi plots.

The IM's local office was at H-302, Ashoka Mews, an apartment complex in upmarket Kondhwa, said the Mumbai crime branch after arresting eight men from the city.

Another revelation is that explosives had been sent to Pune. The police said two men arrested in Mangalore had visited Surat twice and Pune once, transporting explosives in small parcels. The explosives in Surat were detected; police are investigating whether the module planned blasts in Pune.

Of those arrested, four are from Kondhwa and one from Kasba Peth, in the heart of the city. IT executive Mohammed Mansoor Akgar Peerbhoy (31), who used the aliases Munawar alias Mannu, is a principal software manager; Mubin (24) alias Salman Kadar Shaikh is a computer science graduate; Asif Bashiruddin Shaikh (22) alias Hasan alias Mehmood is a mechanical engineer from Pune.

The rest include Mohammed Akbar Ismail Choudhary (26), Majid Akhtar Sheikh (27) and Aniq Shakeel Sayyad (27) and Farooq Shamshuddin Tarkash (25), all from Kondhwa, besides Yasir Anees Sayyed (20) of Kasba Peth.

A member of Choudhary's family said, "We are in deep distress." Choudhary reportedly drove the computer experts to spots where they could identify WiFi networks.

Majid's elder brother, Nazim Sheikh, said Majid and his friends Farooq and Aniq were innocent.

"Majid is a very simple, quiet boy, busy with his job, family and namaz. He has very few friends... all were good people," Nazim said. Majid is an arts graduate from Poona College, worked with Infosys at Hinjewadi and learnt computers while working closely with an architect.

"Majid, Aniq and Farooq ran Acme — which had a computer institute, a mobile shop and an English coaching centre — in Pune Camp. Aniq, working with an IT company, is a college friend while Farooq is a childhood friend. Yasir was working at the mobile shop," Nazim said.

Majid's mother said, "He came home once a week. We were worried when he did not come for a long time and we could not reach him on the mobile. Suddenly, the police said they had arrested him," she said.

Yasir's father Anees said, "My son is innocent. When he didn't return home, we filed a missing report; only then did we realise he had been arrested."

Heading: 100 cops in 15 vehicles sent to pick up one lawyer - Indian Express
Content:
It was originally a plan set to kick off before the Commonwealth Youth Games. Meeting the deadline before the CYG starts on October 12 seems unlikely. The Geographical Information System (GIS)-based project, being started by the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC), will nevertheless be available to citizens. But for that, they will have to wait at least till December.

It's part of the PMC's continuing effort to provide Information Technology (IT) enabled services. "The GIS facility is to help any citizen locate destinations and routes online. The plan was to introduce it before the games. The delay in approval has made it unlikely," PMC Chief Information Officer Anupam Saraph said.

Data on hospitals, multiplexes, malls, gardens, parks, restaurants historical places has been collected for the base map available with the PMC, but the work to host it on the web was delayed as the proposal had been pending since May, he said.

The first phase will be over by December and queries of citizens related to routes and locations, availability of public transport system and cycle tracks will be addressed through it, Saraph said. Citizens will be able to find the nearest garden, multiplex, shopping centre, bank, hospital or school at the click of a button.

The PMC would initially allow citizens to add to missing locations on the map, he said.

The facility has multiple benefits and various departments of the civic body can also use it to give information of ongoing works, Saraph said. The dates on which the works are being undertaken can be displayed on the base map and the other departments as well as citizens can access it instead of calling up civic officials, he added .

Heading: Several mental patients back home, move to make things still better - Indian Express
Content:
Some lawyers had beaten up inspector; fraternity calls it revenge arrest

A hundred policemen in 15 vehicles swooped down on the Parvati home of advocate Rajendra Shinde on Sunday night and arrested him while he was in his underwear. They took him to Shivajinagar police station for interrogation, said his family members.

The police action came around 11.30 in the night. Shinde was booked under Section 353 of the IPC for obstructing a government servant on duty. When Shinde was brought to the court premises on Monday, he was crying loudly and alleging that the police had thrashed him severely during interrogation.

Many lawyers believe the police action was in retaliation to an attack on a police inspector on Saturday.

Some lawyers had allegedly roughed up assistant police inspector Ashok Randive on the premises of the Shivajinagar district and sessions court. In a statement to the Principal District and Sessions Judge A S Cheema on Saturday, Randive had said, "Shinde asked me to reach the court. When I reached the place, I was roughed up by 10-12 lawyers including Shinde and taken before the Principal District and Sessions Judge. Shinde had called me because I had gone to his place to make enquires about him."

The enquiries were apparently in connection with earlier cases against Shinde. On October 2, Shinde had been booked by the Bund Garden police under Sections 323 and 504 of the IPC and on September 8, he had been booked under Sections 323, 504, and 427 of the IPC by the Pune Station police. The charges ranged from voluntarily causing hurt to hurling insults intended to provoke breach of peace.

Shinde, on the other hand, claims Randive reached the court premises on Saturday to arrest him. He alleged that Randive was not in his uniform and did not have an I-card at the time. In connection with the case against him, Shinde said he had already filed an anticipatory bail. Shinde had been granted time till October 7.

But on Sunday night, apparently on the orders of the Police Commissioner, policemen from Duttawadi, Shivajinagar and Bund Garden police stations reached Shinde's house and arrested him. Shinde's family alleged that the police thrashed him before arresting him. They also said the cops damaged the door of the house besides some furniture. They added that Shinde's three-year-old daughter fell unconscious when she was accidentally hit by a policeman.

Shinde was produced in the court of the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate S Dhawale on Monday. There was a heavy police bandobast around the court, as the police feared a backlash from the lawyers. Shinde was released on bail on a personal bond of Rs 10,000.

Heading: After wowing 9 states, youth relay baton arrives in town - Indian Express
Content:
On World Mental Health Day on October 10, the Maharashtra Institute of Mental Health (MIMH) plans to set up self-help groups for the first time at its campus at Sassoon General Hospital to rehabilitate people with mental health problems. This is expected to go a long way in addressing mental health issues, an area of grave concern with eight to ten new patients being admitted to the Regional Mental Hospital (RMH) at Yerawada every day.

But there is some good news too. More than 100 patients admitted to RMH have recovered from their illness this year and have been sent back home. Besides, the number of patients who were not taken back by relatives has also gone down.

Medical Superintendent at RMH, Yerawada, said the hospital had 1,700 patients at present, which was much below its capacity of 2,500 inmates. This year, over 100 patients who recovered were sent back home. Only ten per cent of the patients were returning, which shows a marked improvement in the situation.

"We conduct follow-ups and send counsellors to the patients' homes in the villages," said Bhailume who has started several programmes on October 4 that will continue till October 10, to create awareness on mental health issues.

Experts are being sent to speak at schools and exhibitions are being held at railway stations and bus-stands. There are lectures and street plays lined up and the hospital has also organised a get-together of patients and their relatives on October 7. For the first time, MIMH is setting up self-help groups for addressing mental health issues of patients.

Families play an important role in treatment and rehabilitation, said Dr Alka Pawar, Director, MIMH. In two-and-a-half-year, the institute's day care centre has helped over 450 patients, said Jitendra Gandhi, a lecturer in psychosocial rehabilitation at MIMH. This year, the theme for the World Mental Health Day is advocacy for global mental health — scaling up services through citizen advocacy and action.

Ronny George, coordinator of Chaitanya Institute of Mental Health, a private organisation that takes care of more than 200 patients at its hostels in Pune and Goa, said that a three-year project was being undertaken in Pune district to sensitise people, mainly schoolteachers, policemen and judicial officers, about mental health issues.

Heading: Towing away vehicles: Cops under scanner - Indian Express
Content:
After traversing thousands of kilometres through nine different states, the Youth Baton Relay (YBR) of the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG) is finally arriving in the host city for a grand welcome. It will complete its 67 day journey which began from New Delhi on August 1. Starting Tuesday, the baton will be on a three-day parade within the city, before heading for the final venue point at Balewadi on October 12.

On Monday, the baton passed through the religious places, Dehu-Alandi, and took a halt at the industrial township of Pimpri-Chinchwad. Having flagged of from New Delhi, the baton has passed through nine different states.

The baton, projecting a three-pronged mission of promotion of Olympic sports, and spreading the messages of green games and save tiger mission, is planned to be given an impressive welcome in the city, as the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC), the CYG organising committee and the district collectorate have chalked out elaborate plans. In the city run, eminent personalities from all walks of life will participate. On October 9, there will be a grand carnival starting from Baburao Sanas ground to Balewadi. The route it would take is: Bajirao Road, Vishrambaug Wada, Vishrambaug Wada, Laxmi Road, Alka Talkies chowk, Deccan, F C Road, Agriculture College, Pune University, Aundh and Baner.

On Tuesday, the YBR will reach Khadki cantonment area and will be brought into the city with a procession of cyclists carrying flags of the 71 participating countries. Later, sporting these flags on boats, the baton is scheduled to reach Bund Garden at 3 pm. After this, it would pass by Deccan College, Alandi Road, Airport Road, Gunjan Talkies chowk, Aga Khan Palace, Ramwadi octroi post, Wadgaon Sheri, Chandan Nagar, Kharadi, Magarpatta Road, Hadapsar, Fatima Nagar, Wanavdi, Ghorpadi, Koregaon Park, Wadia College chowk, Pune Station and would reach B J Medical ground by 8 pm where cultural events have been organised to give it a welcome.

The Euphoria band, led by Palash Sen, would present a musical night at the ground. After this, the baton would head for Rajeev Gandhi Zoological Park in Katraj, where it would make a night sojourn.

Addressing the media, MP Suresh Kalmadi said, "The CYG served as a golden opportunity for Pune to build up its infrastructure and I am happy that all the necessary infrastructure is in place. Besides good roads, we have got good signages, high quality streetlights. I hope, all this development brings in more business for the city, with multinational companies setting up their bases here."

Kalmadi said that cities in Maharashtra, which have given a warm welcome to the baton relay, would be given an honour of welcoming the torch of the Commonwealth Games, to be held in New Delhi in 2010. "Many places like Aurangabad, Nagpur, Baramati and Indapur, received the baton with great pomp, hence, I would make a request the Commonwealth Games authorities to carry the torch through these cities in 2010."

He said that Pune, too would welcome the baton in a sparkling manner.

The journey so far
* Among the many modes of transportation, the baton took to the sea route as 101 swimmers took the baton from the Gateway of India in Mumbai to Uran, covering the distance of seven nautical miles. In Jhansi, the vintage cars carried the baton, while in Goa, 'Santa Monica', a boat, was used.
* The baton also visited famous religious places like the Durgah of Khwaja Garib Nawaz in Ajmer, Vitthal temple in Pandharpur, Bhavani Mata temple in Tuljapur, Guru Govindsingh Gurudwara in Nanded, Saibaba temple in Shirdi and temple of Gajanan Maharaj in Shegaon.
* The YBR passed through a few tiger sanctuaries like Sariska in Rajasthan, Sanjay Gandhi National Park in Borivali, Pench in Nagpur, Tadoba in Chandrapur and Melghat region in Amaravati

Heading: ‘Sense of giving among youth lacking’ - Indian Express
Content:
DCP (Traffic) justifies dacoity charge against citizens; lawyers, experts say police overstepping limits

While the city police continue to justify their action of slapping dacoity charge against 10 persons after a scuffle over lifting of vehicles from a no parking zone, lawyers, experts and civic activists have raised objections to the very act of the police relating to lifting of vehicles from no parking zones.

Even as lawyers describe the police action as "an act of theft," experts point out that sensible implementation of rules is required from the police department. Shockingly, the police emphasise that they will keep filing slapping dacoity charge in such cases.

Subhashchandra Bhosale, former president of the Pune Advocates Bar Association, said the dacoity charge against 10 persons shows how the police are using the powers bestowed upon them. "Pen, paper, power, all is theirs. And they are using it as they want," he said. Bhosale said the citizens in this matter can file a case of theft against the policemen. "There is no law which says police can take away vehicles of citizens parked on road. Nobody has the right to take away another's property," he said.

Advocate Sushil Mancharkar said the Motor Vehicle Act does not mention anywhere that police have the right to lift a vehicle parked on the road. "Section 197 of the Motor Vehicle Act says whoever commits the offence and whoever abets the offence of lifting a vehicle without the consent of the owner and in good faith is punishable with a jail term of three months," Mancharkar pointed out.

However, Chandmal Parmar, chairman of the Road and Rail Traffic Management of the MCCIA, said under the Police Act, the Deputy Commissioner of Police can issue a notification regarding a no-parking zone. "Vehicles which affect smooth flow of traffic can be removed by the police. But to avoid confusion regarding the parking zone, the police should place two boards -- one at the starting point and the other at the end." He said he has already taken up this issue with Municipal Commissioner Praveensinh Pardeshi.

Describing the police action of slapping dacoity charge as uncalled for, Parmar said the police towing vans are in a hurry to collect target money. "Certain percentage of the money so collected is shared by the police and the boys lifting vehicles..." he alleged. Yet another aspect which is not considered seriously, said Parmar, is about proper markings of zebra crossing. "At most places, there is no such markings. The police and the civic authorities should coordinate to implement this norm."

Parmar said it is often observed that the constable accompanying the towing van never gets down from the vehicle when the action is taken at a no parking zone. "The boys who have little knowledge of the law or the norms are seen hurriedly lifting vehicles and dumping in the vans. Actually, the constable should get down and see it to that proper action is carried out at the spot," he said. Another traffic expert Prashant Inamdar said the police are making a laughing stock of themselves. "There is no doubt that the police action is wrong. The police can remove vehicles obstructing traffic flow, but the cops should strike a sensible balance..You have to understand the difference when you act against a criminal and a citizen. The police should apply itself when acting against what they consider are traffic offenders."

Justifying the police action, Deputy Commissioner of Police (traffic) Manoj Patil said the court will decide whether the police were right or wrong in applying the dacoity charge. "If such acts are repeated, we will keep filing the dacoity charge," he warned. When asked as to under which Section of the Motor Vehicle Act the police initiates action of towing away citizens vehicles, Patil said it is done under Section 127 of the Motor Vehicle Act which empowers police to tow away vehicles.

Heading: 11 parking lots and PMPML buses to Balewadi - Indian Express
Content:
"The need of the hour is to make the youth of our country natural givers and that can only happen when the education system takes charge to instill the sense of giving in them from childhood," said India's first woman IPS officer Kiran Bedi who was in the city to felicitate the participating NGOs at Yellow Ribbon Pre Diwali NGO fair.

A recipient of Ramon Magsaysay Award (1994) for her reforms in Tihar Jail,Bedi, said that the energy of the youth is not channelised to the right straits because they are not getting right guidance. Quoting her experience on the spirit of giving, Bedi said " I would have been a still pond, ageing and decaying if I would have kept my earnings to myself. But that is not the case. I feel like I progressing with every penny I spend. This what the youth too should feel today. It's not a preaching by me but researches have proved the one who gives at the end of the day is content and happy and this point should be driven home."

Bedi who hosts a radio show on Delhi's radio channel Meow and is the arbitrator in the show Aap ki kachehri on Star Plus said, " Earlier I used to work to earn now my priorities have changed. I earn to work now. These shows that I do I earn from them and use it to run my NGOs." To Bedi the shows are also a medium to reach out to the people to motivate them to come forward for a cause. " I also work in them because this way the message goes from one to million."

The founder of two NGOs, Navjyoti and India Vision Foundation, Bedi, speaking on the occasion advocated the need of bringing the NGOs under one roof. "For space, recognition and visibility it is very important for them to come under one roof. I know what it takes to establish an NGO. Its existence is always under threat. They all should come together so that they voice their efforts loud and clear," said Bedi who actively participates in the NGO fairs across the nation.

Heading: Summit 2008: Hosts MIT win general championship - Indian Express
Content:
A fire due to gas leak in a house on Sunday night at Lohiyanagar slum near Magarpatta city at Hadapsar left one dead and 18 injured, many of whom sustained serious burn injuries.

Kanta Salgar (19) lost her life in the incident. Ten out of the 18 injured were admitted to Surya hospital while five were admitted to Sassoon hospital while some were admitted to a private hospital. PSI DS More of the Hadapsar police station said that " All of the 19 people injured in the accident were immediately rushed to the hospital. Some of them were shifted to the Sassoon and Surya hospital."

Fire brigade officials said that they rushed within 20 minutes after the incident occurred.

The incident occurred at 11 p.m. at Gorakh Madane's house when some of their family friends had come to see his wife Neela, who was ill. The toll was high as the families of Gajre, Londhe, Kondhare and Salgar families were at Madane's residence when the incident happened, said the police officials. Police officials said that as the fire spread so quickly that nobody got a chance to escape. Also, the intensity of the fire was so high that some people standing outside the house were also injured.

Heading: Horizon escape - Indian Express
Content:
After proving a helping hand for the students, FUEL now progresses to include parents and guide them to become stronger support for their wards

By the time Maharashtra worked hard its way to take its literacy rate from 64.87 percent to 77.27 percent in 2001, the criteria to measure a state's development also changed, though not officially. A not-so-bad position seemed indeed a bad one, with the state witnessing the problem of unemployment as any other state would. Among many big reasons there was a small one, and that was of a baffled students' community. While the big reasons were addressed by encouraging primary education in rural belt, the small reason was addressed by the youth, who by this time had understood their dilemma.

Friends Union for Energising Lives (FUEL) is an outcome of one such attempt made to help give direction to aimless students community. Right from the time of its inception in 2006, the organisation has been untiringly working towards enlightening the students with information and helping them in not getting carried away by alluring offers at a wrong time.

After registering huge success in every endeavour, FUEL is now all set to expand their target area and now include parents in their realm of dealings.

"So far we have been concentrating on students. From our experience, we have learnt that parents have a lot more potential to help their child grow better. They can prove to be the strongest support system for the child. So this time, along with the students we would also take parents into consideration and guide them to help their ward," says Shashank Lunkad, development head, FUEL.

On its second anniversary, on October 12, the organisation is releasing their fourth edition of the students FUEL book. The book would contain information about engineering, medical, pharmacy, biotechnology, management, NDA and many more.

Emphasising on the need of counseling for parents Ketan Deshpande, chairman, FUEL, says that from their experience they have come to know that parents play an equally important, or sometime more important role in choosing a course or filling a form and if not guided properly they might end up making mistake, which would cost dear to the students in future.

"Parents can make it much easier for the students by giving them right information. We have seen that buying of forms is usually done by parents while filling up of the same is jointly done by the students and parent. Presumptions may lead to many wrong decisions so we need to tell them how can they help their child while he or she prepares for the tests," says Deshpande.

Apart from helping the students with admission process, FUEL also gives one to one counseling to the students in need. Their help line number is open for the students for instant help if they get stuck anywhere while filling a form.

Heading: Munnabhai MP? - Indian Express
Content:
She paints women, their relationships and their inner space, while serving up a colourful palette of traditional Mithila paintings with an urban twist. Shelly Jyoti, a self-taught artist, displays both skill and sensitivity while dealing with her medium of acrylic and ink on archival paper. "I have always been interested in the decorative aspect of art. I add my own personal narratives to a style of painting, I feel I am bringing tradition alive," says the Baroda-based painter, who was born in Delhi in the year 1957.

She is having her first solo in Mumbai—Beyond Mithila: Exploring the Decorative at Jamaat Art Gallery in Colaba (Mumbai). "As far as I go, Mithila appeals to my senses, rather than my intellect. I also think it's important to reconnect with art done by women, involving art that welcomes ornamentation instead of eschewing it," says Jyoti.

Mithila is relegated to the realm of craft but many contemporary artists are revisiting the style and imbuing it with new narratives.

"When I was invited last year by Women Made Art Gallery, in Chicago, I felt that I wanted to share the heritage of India with the people in America," says Jyoti who had a hearty response with 250 people turning up for the opening at the gallery.

"My current body of work explores a new medium, Zardozi textile, block printing with some of the motifs I use in my paintings," says Jyoti who also writes poems to accompany her paintings. They read as a lyrical artist's statement about the works.

In one of them she compares her mother to a tree.

"My next show is looking at a more political issue, the narratives of Indigo workers, who have been exploited through during Colonial times," says the artist who plans to collaborate with an American artist. "Collaboration is good because it brings in different cultural contexts and I am always open to fusion. However, much about this show is yet to be decided," says the artist who prices her paintings between Rs 3,500 to Rs 1 lakh.

Heading: Victorian ways - Indian Express
Content:
With 20 films under his belt, at a reported fee of Rs 12 crore each, a new production house and political ambitions ahead, meet the new and improved Sanjay Dutt

A career going great guns and a seemingly happy personal front, life is coming up roses for Sanjay Dutt. Kidnap, his first big film of 2008, released on Thursday and the actor has a long line-up of films like Blue, EMI and Aladin in the last quarter of the year.

Dutt has also turned a producer with the launch of his own banner, Sanjay Dutt Productions. Two films, an action adventure directed by Soham Shah and another action film directed by Milan Luthria, are scheduled to hit the floors next year. Talks are also on with five more directors, which make it seven films in all. And Dutt will act in all of these.

The 49-year-old is also committed to a couple of film assignments for Balaji Films. In all, the actor has almost 20 films in various stages of production. "I'm very charged about life and want to do a lot of good work. Thankfully, I'm still getting it," he says with characteristic nonchalance.

There are other things that Dutt is contemplating. Promoting boxing is one, ever since Vijender Singh got home the medal from the Beijing Olympics. And trying his hand at politics is also on his wish-list, but that when the work pressure is less.

Directing a film is also part of his future plans. "I haven't yet thought about it seriously, but I will definitely be taking it up in the near future," he confides.

In Kidnap, the high action drama, has him essay a multi-millionaire whose daughter is held for ransom. The role is special for Dutt. It is for the first time that the actor is playing father to a teenage girl, close to his daughter's age. This is one of the reasons he was considered for the role. "Sanjay Gadhvi saw me with my daughter Trishala on a show and said that he could think of no one but me to play the part."

"There are times in a person's life when all the money in the world can be of no use. Working for this high drama between father and daughter was a very emotional experience for me. I also enjoyed working with Imran Khan who I found to be a very confident actor and a grounded person," Dutt says.

The actor hotly denies that relations between him and his daughter are strained because of his marriage to Manyata. "Trishala was with us in the Bahamas when I was shooting there for Blue, and even otherwise we are on the Net every day. She also shares everything she does with me. She is studying Forensic Sciences and just the other day she called to say that there was a dead body with a bullet in its head lying in front of her. She appeared so cool about it, but it really blew my mind," he smiles indulgently.

Heading: Ready or not, here it comes - Indian Express
Content:
English is not just another language. It is also an important tool that helps one go higher in the profession

Help me madam, please ek shoe box kharid do, meri life ban jayegi, maine food nahi khaya subah se," says seven-year-old Ajay. Ajay, who has never been to a school, lives in Swargate and earns his living by polishing shoes at the busy MG Road. When asked how he knows words from English laguange, he says, "English to bolna padega, warna customer nahi aate. Jyada kamane keliye hi thoda English sikha."

Ajay is not the sole example who feels English makes a lot of difference to business. Many masters of their own trade also feel the same.

Take for example, the real estate agents, who master the art of marketing, but many a time, find it difficult to impress a client without a considerable knowledge of English.

Anil Nair, real estate agent, says, "We are, no doubt, expected to speak in English in order to impress the client, at least for the first time. The mentality of judging a person's knowledge from his familiarity with English is very much there in the market. At times people evaluate you by this criterion. Particularly when dealing for commercial buildings, we do need to make an impact on a client by speaking refined English and thus appear smart."

More than developing as a language, English is seen as an important tool that helps you go higher in your profession.

Owner of Yashraj Group (real estate), Rohit Purohit says, "English is though a mere formality, but its importance cannot be denied. English is more for show off, but where actual dealing is concerned, Hindi is best. But we certainly cannot do without English as that brings the business, well not all the time."

Another set of professionals who off late are facing problem because of their limited spoken English knowledge is aspiring politicians or social organisations' members.

Noordin Somji, member, NSUI, says, "English has undoubtedly become a necessity. Our focus is students, their problem and their social responsibility and English, it seems, is the mother tongue of students. Given large number of non-Marathi speaking students, we do at times need to talk in English. However, Marathi and Hindi suffices but we cannot neglect English, which is not only necessary for proper communication but also for our growth."

Let alone, professionals, the new-generation autowalas leave no stone unturned in impressing the customer by their linguistic skill. "Abhi English to bolna padta hai na, aajkal foreigner hi nahi apne logo ke liye bhi English bolna padta hai," says Sudhir Khadilkar, who runs an autorickshaw in the city. After facing a lot of problem in the initial years, Khadilkar learnt the trick later and started talking to his customer in English. "I cannot speak very good English, but I can manage to impress the passenger with this. My knowledge of English, though limited, helps me in getting regular passengers," says Khadilkar, who limits his conversation to basic queries like – Where to go? How much money to pay? For answering some basic queries of the passenger when they ask.

Vijay, an autowala, had to learn English to impress his passengers in Koregaon Park area. "Yahan to bahut saare foreigners hai or North east se hai, unko Hindi or Marathi nahi samajhta hai. Or agar maine English nahi sikha to business nahi chalega," says Vijay.

Given a large number of willing-to-learn people, there has been a strong market for the institutes that teach spoken English skill.

Heading: Navratra heats up caste cauldron - Indian Express
Content:
Many say that the Commonwealth Youth Games starting on October 12 is the best opportunity Pune has had to showcase herself globally. Political rivals say it is the last throw of the dice by Suresh Kalmadi to hold on to his constituency. For Puneites, it was a chance to see their city get a makeover. In this series, The Indian Express will analyse the various aspects of the build-up to the event and see what the people of the city have gained in the bargain.

In the first part, NISHA NAMBIAR interviews Kalmadi on the preparations and progress...

With days left for the Games, is Pune 100 per cent ready to host them?
Yes, Pune is getting ready. Work inside the stadium and on civic infrastructure has been completed on schedule. I am happy with the progress. We still have some days to go and the final touches will be given in these days. We have the best sports infrastructure and we have the Olympic team coming down to help us for various events. We are making sure that everything is in place.

What about the city's civic infrastructure? Is it ready?
Yes, the four roads leading to the sports city have been done up. The much-talked-about Baner Road is ready. The media hype created about the delay in work, especially on this road, can be laid to rest now. The alternative road, Sus Road, too is ready; so are the approach road from Mumbai to Karve road via Chandni Chowk and the airport road.

The Centre recently released an extra Rs 43.5 crore. How is this going to be used?
This will be mainly for the organising committee to make various arrangements and stage various functions for the event.

How much funds have been utilised for the Games?
We got Rs 2,500 crore from the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission. I had Union Urban Development Minister Jaipal Reddy visit the site and an extra Rs 500 crore was released. We spent Rs 2,500 crore on civic infrastructure and Rs 500 crore on the stadium.

Where have the maximum funds been allotted?
Roadwork took up the major chunk, followed by BRTS, riverside development, slum rehab, drainage on certain stretches and green islands.

How were the results of the green sports theme?
The aim was to reduce environmental pollution; I think we have been largely successful. A green council with R K Pachauri and Shashi Tharoor on the panel was formed looking ahead at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. We started the movement; it will be taken up from here.

How much was allocated for green sports?
Around Rs 5 crore was used for spreading the message. We stressed eco-construction, solar lighting and heating, rain harvesting and landscaping, environmental awareness in schools and e-waste management in colleges. We have set up biodiversity and theme parks and arranged CNG buses and battery-operated vehicles to ferry people to the stadium. Posters on the green Games too have been put up and I am happy with the way the message has been spread.

With the Met department forecasting rain, are the Games ready to face that?
We are equipped to counter the rain. Most of the events are indoors; for the rest we will make arrangements.

Are you happy the way Pune will be showcased?
This event will put Pune on the global map. We have done all we can to present the city at its best. These last few days will see the Games being promoted as a brand.

Earlier you had said that you are not looking at CYG as a revenue-raising event…
Yes. We look at it as an opportunity to showcase Pune.
