Content:
Media wing of Indian mujahideen: Two of them travelled to Mumbai from Pune to send terror e-mails just before blasts

The arrest of 15 more men by Mumbai Police in connection with a string of bomb blasts across the country and the busting of the "media wing" of the Indian Mujahideen had laid bare a network of "educated men from respectable families", some of them with "highly paid salaries", working in tandem to wreak havoc, officials said on Monday.

Prominent among the 15 are Mohammed Mansoor Asghar Peerbhoy (31), a computer engineer who worked for an MNC, and Mubin alias Salman Kadar Shaikh (24), a computer science graduate. Both allegedly travelled all the way from Pune to Mumbai to send terror e-mails just minutes before blasts. The Indian Mujahideen had spent around "Rs 70,000 in training these two in hacking" said Rakesh Maria, Joint Commissioner of Police (crime).

While investigators were probing the terror e-mails, it was an interrogation report of an Azamgarh accused, Shahbaz, by Rajasthan Police which first indicated the presence of a separate media wing. "It was in the third e-mail that the group emphasised that they have a media wing working purely on the publicity front," said Hemant Karkare, Joint Commissioner of Police, Anti-Terrorism Squad.

The idea of sending e-mails was to claim credit for the terror blasts, which, they have allegedly told investigators, was Riyaz Bhatkal's way of getting more attention and thus more funds from people with similar criminal intentions. The media wing's second threat e-mail sent from Khalsa College's unsecured wi-fi network was "to deride authorities and get them off track (from investigation)," adds Maria.

While Peerbhoy worked with an MNC and earned Rs 19 lakh per year, Mubin comes from a very educated background and his English skills were used to polish the final copies. Peerbhoy and Mubin took briefs on the content from Riyaz Bhatkal and Iqbal Bhatkal before they drafted and converted them into PDF formats.

According to Maria, the three had earlier conducted separate recce trips looking for unsecured wi-fi networks across the city on five occasions in areas like Sion, Chembur, Chatrapati Shivaji Terminus and Sanpada. On July 26, the day of the Ahmedabad blasts, the group had been told to send the terror e-mail at 18:40 hours. The three were driven down to Mumbai from Pune by driver and an Indian Mujahideen member Mohammed Akbar Ismail Chaudhary alias Yakub (28) in a blue Esteem.

The second e-mail was allegedly to shift attention and delay the investigation. The brief for the third e-mail, timed for the New Delhi blast, was also given in the same manner with the despatch time at 18:20 hours, adds Maria. The same vehicle was used in all three instances, he adds. The group would split and take the laptops with them in state transport buses to avoid checking after their task was accomplished.

Five laptops, including the ones used for sending the e-mails, six central processing units, three pen drives and equipment for tracking radio frequency and wi-fi routers were seized from the group. The probe will focus on the source of the contents of the mail. "We are aware that some of the contents were cut paste jobs," adds Karkare.

Youngest of them, 19-yr-old Javed, was also among highly 'indoctrinated'

Nineteen-year-old Javed Mohammed Ali is the youngest among the 15 new faces of terror and according to senior crime branch officials, he is among "the highly indoctrinated".

"It was Javed who led us to all the Mangalore arrests," said Deven Bharti, Additional Commissioner of Police, (crime), "His statement is crucial as he has admitted that Riyaz Bhatkal even stayed at their home."

Javed, according to the crime branch, had been in touch with many of the other accused and was aware of their roles, and it was he who led the investigation to the other module members. He has been accused of being a criminal conspirator.

While many of the older men were foot soldiers and were involved in transporting cars and gelatin sticks, Javed, was also actively involved in training programmes, investigators said.

The group had assigned him the role of a "courier" as his age was an advantage. He was used many times to transport essential items and also act as a communicator between group members. His father, Mohammed Ali Ahmed (44), a civil contractor in Mangalore, has been charged with harbouring terrorists and helping them in their activities by providing a safe house.

Javed, who is proficient in Arabic studies, was aware of all the movements in the house and actively participated in the conspiracy sessions, according to the crime branch. The training literature used instances of atrocities against Muslims and evidence collected included Jihadi literature allegedly in Javed's handwriting.

Heading: Sleuths posed as patrons to identify peddlers - Indian Express
Content:
Nine charged with possessing, selling drugs, rest released after taking samples; Ecstasy tablets, LSD, charas seized

A team of Anti-Narcotics Cell sleuths on Sunday night raided a pub in Juhu and detained 239 youths attending an alleged rave party there. Nine of those detained were later arrested on charges of possessing, sale and consumption of narcotics. The police seized around 104 tablets of Ecstasy, 850 drops of LSD and charas worth around Rs 9.6 lakh.

The team was led by Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) Vishwas Nangre-Patil, who is known for his crack-down on rave parties in Pune.

According to Nangre-Patil, the cell received information that the pub, Bombay 72 degrees East, located near Prithvi theatre was hosting a trance party where narcotics were being used. "Based on the information, we staked out the place for a few days and on getting evidence that narcotics were being circulated, we raided the premises on the night of Sunday. In the raid, we seized drugs and Rs 1.56 lakh in cash. Out of the 239 people detained during the raid, eight, including a woman, were found to be in possession of narcotics and have been arrested. As for the rest, they were sent to various government hospitals for getting their blood and urine samples and were released later."

The samples will be sent to Kalina laboratory for testing and once the results are available, action will be taken against those test positive for usage of narcotics, Nangre-Patil said. "However, our main focus was on apprehending the peddlers. The youths who were present at the party are victims of this vice and they were not treated like criminals at all," he said.

The nine arrested have been identified as Rahul Karmarkar, Ben Simone, an Israeli national and the DJ of the trance party, Rajesh Talwar, Salil Roy, Wheelan Bretto, Sameer Shah, Salil Kothari, Kashish Malkani and Anuradha.

When asked to comment on the speculation that some of the people present at the party belonged to the families of Bollywood personalities, Patil said, "Like we have said, the youths have been treated as victims and hence, I do not want to disclose the identities of any of them unless and until their test results are out."

The arrested will be produced before the magistrate's court on Tuesday, Patil said. "The Israeli DJ, who was here on a work visa, was also involved in the peddling racket and we have informed the Special Branch about this. Our investigation will now also look at the angle of how these peddlers got the drugs and will crack down on the source," he said.

Heading: Zubin the son returns to pay homage to his father - Indian Express
Content:
It was an elaborate operation by the Anti-Narcotics Cell, in which sleuths posed as patrons, that helped bust the trance party at a Juhu pub on Sunday night. First to enter the party were three sleuths in plain clothes.

"We had to make sure that these decoys looked like regular party-goers, otherwise they would have been easily made out. Hence the officers chosen for this mission were young men who could dress and look like regular party-goers," said DCP Vishwas Nangre-Patil, who led the raid.

Recollecting an incident that he had experienced a few days before the raid, he said: "A couple of days before we sent the decoys, I along with a female officer, dressed in civilian clothes, had entered the same pub where the raid was carried out later. However, the minute we entered, we could sense a subtle change in the mood and temperament of the crowd. My guess is that the peddlers who were present in the place could identify me as a police officer, due to my moustache and my hair-cut."

Not wanting to take a chance on the second occasion, Nangre-Patil sent a batch of young officers dressed like 20-something party-goers to identify the peddlers. Once the peddlers were identified and the other sleuths posted outside were signalled about their presence and they moved in for the raid.

Asked how the under-cover officers identified the peddlers, Nangre-Patil said, "These under-cover officers are professionals and are very much aware of the ways of the drug peddlers at such places. Usually, the peddlers who operate at such parties wear a distinctive item of clothing, which is like a uniform for the peddlers, and the potential buyer knows who to approach. For example, in some places, a peddler might wear a T-shirt bearing the image of a skull and cross-bones, which identifies him as a peddler to the other patrons of the pub so that they can approach him."

Heading: Healing breaches with music  - Indian Express
Content:
To mark Mehli Mehta's birth centenary, the conductor will hold a series of concerts in the city of his birth

Zubin Mehta will take to the stage this week to mark the birth centenary of his late father Mehli Mehta, an accomplished violinist and founder of the Bombay Symphony Orchestra, by conducting a series of concerts in the city.

The concert series, organised by the Mehli Mehta Foundation, will see Mehta returning to the city of his birth to honour his father, along with The Israel Philharmonic Orchestra and classical music stalwarts — pianist and conductor Daniel Barenboim, tenor Placido Domingo, violinist and conductor Pinchas Zukerman, soprano Barbara Frittoli, cellist Amanda Forsyth and pianist Tatiana Goncharova. The announcement came at a press conference at the Taj Mahal Palace and Tower on Monday.

The proceeds from the concert would go to Mehli Mehta Foundation which is planning to open a school to nurture the best of Indian music talent. "We don't want the Indian youth to go abroad to study music and then never come back," Mehta said, adding, "We cannot compete with China and Japan, of course, since they have wholeheartedly embraced western classical music. In comparison, India is still deeply involved with Indian music."

The plan for the school is still in the initial stages. "Hopefully we'll raise enough money from the concerts and from private donors, to turn our dream into reality. We'll be looking for the best teachers from all over the world for the school," Zubin said.

The concerts will feature pieces that Mehli Mehta had performed during his lifetime. "My father would have turned 100 last week and my mother will turn 100 next week," said Mehta, "That is why we chose this week for our visit." Mehta expressed his gratitude to his friends and colleagues for coming to India to perform in his father's memory.

"My friends have been telling me for years that they want to perform in India. Barbara (Frittoli) had to cancel a recital in Vienna because we asked her at the last moment. And the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra is playing four of these concerts without remuneration."

Barenboim spoke about his desire to perform at the centenary concerts and his attachment to the Mehta family. "Zubin is more than a colleague... he's almost like a brother to me," he said.

Mehta also spoke about how Mumbai has changed over the years. "This used to be a beautiful city," he said. "Every city grows. We have to be practical about that. But we also have to act responsibly. I hate to go to Cuffe Parade now, where I was born and brought up. The fishing village there could've been made very charming. Instead, it has been allowed to stagnate. And just last week there was an article in a newspaper which made for a sad reading. I live abroad as a proud Indian and it makes me very sad when I read articles like that."

Heading: Education key to women empowerment: Sule - Indian Express
Content:
It may seem strange to others, but to Daniel Barenboim, there is nothing bizarre about holding both an Israeli and a Palestinian passport. "I'm neither anti-Israel nor I'm anti-Palestine," he clarifies. Barenboim is in Mumbai along with conductor Zubin Mehta for the series of concerts to mark the centenary of Mehta's father, Mihli Mehta.

A Jew, born in 1942 at the height of the Holocaust, Barenboim has worked closely with three German orchestras, the Berlin Philharmonic, the Staatskapelle Berlin and the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra. The Argentine-born musician is Israeli by nationality and makes it very clear that he has no political agenda and that for him, it's all about music.  

The ace pianist is certainly a pioneer of sorts. He's the first person to be granted both Israeli and Palestinian citizenship and had established the West-Eastern Divan orchestra along with the American-Palestinian intellectual, the late Edward.

"The orchestra consists of people from all over the Middle East, Israel, Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Tunisia and Palestine," he says adding, "when people play music together, they become dependent on each other. It's not like reading literature, which you can do on your own. Making music requires you to be in co operation with other people."  

Barenboim has been a vocal commentator on the middle-eastern situation. "Both Israelis and Palestinians believe that they have the right to live on the same little piece of land. The Israelis are convinced that the Palestinians are trying to push them into the sea and the Palestinians feel that the Israelis are trying to push them into the desert."  

The maestro says that he doesn't believe that a military solution is likely to solve the political impasse in the region. But he also stresses that music is not likely to do the same either. "It's not a political solution," he explains. "It's a humane solution. Music brings people closer to each other and hopefully, it'll lead to greater co operation," he adds.

Heading: Panel: Corporator submitted fake documents to contest election - Indian Express
Content:
'We politicians should be made accountable. Only way of doing this by excercising right to vote'

Rajya Sabha MP Supriya Sule poured her heart out on the issues that most bother her to a group of young women from the Ladies' wing of Indian Merchants' Chamber (IMC) on Monday. Pioneering the cause of micro-finance and enabling women come out of their shell in rural Maharashtra through Self-help groups (SHGs), Sule stated that the whole concept can succeed only if there is proper mapping of things done by SHGs. "It is not just enough for SHGs to manufacture a product. It should be promoted well and quality should be ensured. Only then can SHGs become a true success story. Also, we need a centralized system as to know how each product is manufactured, from where it comes and how it is made," said Sule.

Only last week Sule had stated how cheaper loan rates will give a boost to SHGs. Following this the state government had declared that banks will finance SHGs at a meager rate of 4%. Sule runs an NGO Yashsawini. 6,000 SHGs are affiliated to it. The NGO recently won an order worth Rs 3.5-crore from retailer Big Bazaar for supply of around 100 products made by it.

Stressing on the fact that women emancipation can succeed only with education, Sule said that despite all the efforts primary education in rural areas is still in an abysmal state. "The latest HRD report shows that though there is 100% enrollment in rural schools at the primary level. The dropout rate increases gradually. While schools report 100% admissions in first standard. By the time a batch reaches 5th standard there is almost a 50% drop out. Primary education is a serious problem especially in rural areas," said Sule.

"The disparity also increases as there is a huge drop out rate among the faculty in rural areas and in many cases faculty themselves are unaware of most issues, we don't need just education but we need skilled, quality education," she added. Sule applauded the Sarva Siksha Abhiyaan and stated that it is indeed the need of the hour.

"The Sarva Siksha Abhiyaan has tremendously changed the nature of elementary education in rural areas. While I admit that no policy can be 100% successful. The scheme has definitely improved primary education in rural pockets," she said. Sule also did not shy away from commenting on language politics rampant in the city.

"It is a sad thing that in a cosmopolitan city like Mumbai, language and caste has become a divisive factor. This was never the case earlier. Mumbai's social fabric is changing. We have always been the city of integration. This should be maintained and political leaders should be refrained from playing language politics," she added.Urging every citizen to vote during the upcoming elections, she stated that ultimately all the power lies in the hands of the voters. "We politicians should be made accountable. The only way the common man can ensure this is by exercising the right to vote," Sule said.

Heading: One electrocuted, 6 injured in Dharavi - Indian Express
Content:
After allegedly faking his caste details and contesting on a fake name, a Kurla corporator may soon lose his seat. The state government's scrutiny committee recently found that the certificate submitted by independent corporator Narayan Janu Pawar was fake and declared that he had furnished false documents to contest under OBC category from ward number 158 of Kurla. As per the committee's findings, Pawar's domicile name is Gangaram.

Complainant Masud Ansari who also contested election on a Congress ticket lost to Pawar by 100 votes. Learning that Pawar had furnished false documents to contest the election, Ansari approached the caste scrutiny committee, which later declared his caste certificate invalid."We had an inkling that Pawar was upto some mischief and filed a complaint with the caste scrutiny committee soon after the election in February last year.

The committee passed an order in our favour and declared that his certificates were invalid," said Ansari.

"Pawar's eligibility to contest elections cannot be established from the documents he had submitted, hence his eligibility stands invalid. He has betrayed the BMC and the public by serving the civic body for over seven years. A case has been registered against Pawar for forgery," reads the committee report.

"Pawar had furnished the details of his primary education. But, my client Ansari knew that he had never attended school. Also, in his daughter's birth certificate, his name is recorded as Gangaram, not Narayan," said Ansari's advocate Anjali Iyer.

When contacted, Pawar said, "We're are moving the High Court now. The committee did not give us ample time to prove the case. The scrutiny was politically driven and hence it's unjust."

Heading: Complications due to drugs in HIV+ patients new challenge, say doctors - Indian Express
Content:
The injured suffered 10-40 percent burns and have been admitted to Sion hospital

A 25-year-old youth died of electrocution after a live cable wire broke and fell atop a house in Dharavi in the wee hours of Monday. Six other were injured in the incident which occurred around 3.15 am.

While Rasul Ajine Khan died instantly, Anwarjehan (40), Sanarat Pawar (42), Yusus Khan (55), Karin Khan (26), Arum Khan (15) and Bismillah Khan (25) suffered 10-40 per cent burns. They are undergoing treatment at the Sion Hospital.

A complaint was made to the Dharavi police by one of a relative of the victims. According to the statement of the complainant, Rasul was standing on the terrace when his hand accidentally brushed against the overhanging cable. The wire broke due to the impact and Rasul came in direct contact with the live wire. A case of death due to negligence has been registered. However, the police are yet to identify the accused in the case.

Heading: Cash & Carry unhappy with Bloc terms - Indian Express
Content:
NACO has revised drug regime under Anti-Retroviral Therapy, but doctors maintain toxicity not fatal

Approximately 600 HIV-positive patients at the state-run J J Hospital and many others in the Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) treatment centres in the country are currently developing toxicity due to the treatment. Recognising this as a grave problem, National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) under its revised national guidelines has recently revised the drug regimen by introducing alternate first line treatment. 

According to NACO, currently there are about 177 ART centres providing first line treatment to over 1.5 lakh patients. Due to the long duration of the treatment, the patients are increasingly experiencing various complications because of ART drugs. However, the doctors say that toxicity in this case does not lead to mortality. The data and information in this regard was presented at the ongoing conference on Fundamental and Transnational Research on HIV and AIDS.

"Increasingly, toxicity of ART is becoming an important issue in the management of patients with HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus). The first line ART treatment has improved the CD4 count (used to assess a person's immune system) and has decreased the incidence of opportunistic infection. But with continued use, the complications of treatment are being seen in an increased frequency in most of the ART centres in the country," said Dr Alaka Deshpande, in-charge of the ART centre at the J J Hospital which is the largest in the country. "Despite toxicity, permanent and good adherence to the therapy is needed to maximize its long-term benefits," Dr Deshpande added.

According to doctors, approximately 10 per cent of patients on the first line of ART treatment are developing toxicity. Although adverse reactions to the therapy are common, and profoundly affect its clinical efficacy by limiting adherence, many such reactions are poorly studied and analysed, and are under-reported, say doctors.

"Toxicity in form of facial disfigurement, buffalo hump due to maldistribution of fat, breast hypertrophy (large breast) in men, thinner limbs, sunken chic, loss of mass on the buttock and protruding belly, peripheral neuropathy (tingling numbness in the limb and burning pain in the feet), is mainly caused due to a drug — Stavudine— introduced in the first line of treatment. Doctors treating HIV patients had no option but to give Stavudine as Zidovudi— alternative drug available in the first line of treatment causes sever anemia. Indian HIV patients anyways have low hemoglobin and are anemic, hence doctors did not have any option but to bank on Stavudine," said Dr Deshpande.

However, NACO last month introduced a new drug in the ART regimen called Tenofovir.

"The drug is expensive but is provided free of cost at the J J Hospital currently and will be provided at selected centres all over the country. Only if other two drugs fail to work, Tenofovir will be used in the form of combination therapy," said Dr Deshpande.

In countries like the US and the UK, Tenofovir is used as the first line drug to treat HIV patients due to the toxicity of the other two drugs. "Zedovudine, least expensive drug, was given accelerated approval by the US Food and Drug Administration in 1987 and Stavudine in 1995. After the continued use, the long term complications are becoming apparent of late. Therefore in the West, they have switched to Tenofovir. India too will slowly shift to the less toxic drug as increased morbidity, escalating cost of management and increased stigmatisation is becoming a new challenge," said Dr Deshpande. The J J Hospital has so far treated 15 patients with Tenofovir.

Heading: Securitymen relieved as Tatas walk out of Singur - Indian Express
Content:
A high-level meeting to resolve the issue of granting a licence to Metro Cash & Carry failed to reach a consensus on Monday. While the state government claimed that the German giant had accepted most of the conditions imposed by the Forward Bloc-controlled APMC, company officials did not confirm it.

The Bloc is demanding that the German major should not be allowed to sell products less than Rs 5000 and the retailers, who will buy from the company, should have a licence from the Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee (APMC). The wholesale giant is, however, against these conditions.

To sort out the issues, a delegation of the company held a meeting with Chief Secretary Amit Kiran Deb at the Writers' Buildings on Monday. Principal Secretary to the chief minister Subesh Das, APMC Chairman Naren Chatterjee and other officials of the agriculture department were also present at the meeting.

After the meeting, Das said the state government will sign a Memorandum of Understanding with the company on October 10. Chatterjee said the company has accepted five of the six conditions that were imposed by the APMC for granting a licence to the company. According to Chatterjee, the conditions were: Metro cannot sell any product that costs less than Rs 5,000; It will never enter into retail business in the state; If any dispute arises between the company and APMC, it will be decided only at a Kolkata court; The company will have to keep the APMC informed about the kind of commodities they will keep in their outlets; The company cannot go for contract farming; They will have to follow the APMC rules, failing which, their licence will be cancelled.

"We could not reach a consensus on the first condition but the company has accepted the remaining ones," Chatterjee said.

The company, however, did not confirm that they have accepted the conditions. "Our discussions are going on. We can say anything only when a decision is taken," Vishal Sehgal, head, corporate communications, Metro Cash & Carry, told The Indian Express.

The issue of granting licence to the German company had created a rift between the CPM, which favoured the granting of the licence and the Forward Bloc, which was against it.

Things came to such a pass that the Bloc had decided to withdraw its ministers from the state Cabinet. The issue was resolved at a Left Front meeting, when it was decided that the company would be issued a licence only if it accepted some conditions.

Heading: ‘Farmers panicked at security excess’ - Indian Express
Content:
The pullout decision by the Tatas has not only brought a smile on Trinamool chief Mamata Banerjee's face, but has also proved to be a boon for the policemen deployed there.

The police camp set up just outside the factory premises wore a deserted look on Monday. The policemen were seen relaxing and engaging in talks and laughter. Sources said that the number of private security personnel who were deployed to guard the factory has also been reduced.

More than 2,000 policemen were pressed into service to guard the Tata small car factory in Singur for the last two years. The policemen were primarily deployed for guarding the boundary wall of the project site. But even after the construction work began at the site, the police remained there to prevent any untoward incident.

Policemen from various districts, who were deployed in Singur, often complained of poor working conditions. Now, with the Tatas deciding to shift the small car project from Singur, there is a sense of relief among the policemen. "I was posted here for the last two years. We seldom got holidays. Now, with the Tatas going away, we might be shifted back to our original postings," said a constable of Murshidabad district.

The number of private security personnel engaged by the Tatas has also gone down. A senior police officer said now the primary focus is on maintaining law and order in Singur villages, as there is palpable tension between the CPM and the Trinamool.

Heading: Exodus of doctors leaves SAI centres in poor health - Indian Express
Content:
Congress leader and former Kolkata mayor Subrata Mukherjee blamed the Left Front government for the Singur fiasco. The imposition of Section 144 of CrPC while taking possession of the land in December 2006 for the Tata Motors' plant had rubbed the dispossessed farmers the wrong way, he said.

"The government deployed armed forces that created panic among the farmers. The boundary wall of the Nano project site was erected when Section 144 was clamped," he said on Monday. "From the very beginning, there was an air of arrogance on the part of the state government. After starting off on the wrong foot, how could the government instill confidence among locals?" Subrata added.

At a public function on Sunday, External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee had said, "Industry cannot come up in air, it has to be set up on land." The observation was contradictory to the stand taken on Singur issue by WBPCC chief Priya Ranjan Dasmunsi and the former mayor. Dasmunsi had earlier demanded that 300 acres of the land should be returned to unwilling farmers in Singur.

"If the state government is ready to return 70 acres from the project area to the farmers, why can't they return 300 acres? We still believe that the plant could have functioned properly without having the ancillary units in close proximity. These units could have been set up on the land opposite the plant site," said the former mayor.

Subrata, a former Trinamool leader, had participated in Trinamool chief Mamata Banerjee's rally in Singur last month and spoken in favour of the dispossessed farmers.

Heading: Rains may dampen spirit of pandal hoppers - Indian Express
Content:
The Union Sports Ministry might be claiming that it wants to establish modern, scientific infrastructure to churn out world-class players, but the efforts put in by the ministry for the purpose prove otherwise.

Twenty-five years ago, the ministry had introduced several centres of Sports Authority of India (SAI) across the country. Considering the present state of affairs, however, it can be said that SAI is far from achieving its goal of churning out top-quality players in any discipline.

A closer look at the miserable condition of the medical centres of SAI centres all over India reveals that there is much left to be desired. Over the last 15 years, there has been an alarming decline in the state and quality of sports science, as well as the condition of doctors at SAI's various centres.

In the early 1990s, a group of 48 qualified doctors had joined different centres of SAI. Since 1993, eighteen of these doctors have resigned from their services. Moreover, it has been learnt that six more highly qualified doctors are mulling leaving SAI soon.

Most of the doctors who have left SAI are currently settled in other circuits and are faring moderately. SAI's top brass, however, still appears reluctant when the topic of revival of the medical front crops up.

When asked about the situation, PSM Chandran who, after retiring recently, is still on contract with the SAI till 2010 as a Senior Scientific Officer (SSO) at its head office in New Delhi admitted that things are far from being alright.

Chandran, who also has been assigned to unofficially monitor all the SAI medical centres in India, told The Indian Express recently: "It is true that the top brass of SAI should have been more careful with the handling of the doctors who have left, who were qualified and deserved honorable positions".

He added: "The key factor that forced them to leave SAI was that there were no promotions. Explaining the situation, we submitted several proposals to the SAI top brass for the revival of medical centres and better handling of doctors. We proposed to increase the number of designations of the doctors at SAI. It is not very nice to say that there are only nine doctors at SAI across the country now. I hope the administration responds to our appeal."

Explaining the reason behind their resignation from SAI, one of the doctors said on condition of anonymity: "The doctors, despite having a high profile and consistent performance, do not get the promotions they deserve. The maximum scope a doctor, joining any SAI centre at the post of Junior Scientific Officer (JSO), has is finishing his career at SAI itself as a Senior Scientific Officer (SSO). As an SSO, your monthly salary won't exceed Rs 15,000".

"Moreover, the corruption in SAI administration at all the centres was also a major factor that forced several qualified and quality doctors to leave," said the doctor.

The Union sports ministry, it seems, is learning from its mistakes, and taking steps to rectify them. For, it is learnt that Chandran's appeal and suggestions to consider the scientific officers' promotion and restructure their financial status have been responded by the SAI top brass. It is believed that the Union sports ministry as well as SAI top brass are in a procedure to restructure the doctors' salary structure, and will implement it from next year.

Heading: Security rules on Saptami as never before - Indian Express
Content:
With rains acting as a spoilsport on the first two days of the Pujas, pandal hoppers are keeping their fingers crossed as they fear that further rains might be a blow for their plans.

"We wanted to visit a few pandals on Sunday. But the rain destroyed our plans and we had to reschedule our pandal hopping spree," said Punit Mukherjee, a Class XI student.

Many visitors who went to Salt Lake for pandal hopping were caught off guard as sudden showers lashed various parts of Salt Lake on Sasthi. The hour-long rain on Sunday across central, northern and eastern Kolkata had left many pandals waterlogged and forced the people to stay indoors.

The Alipore Meteorological Department has, meanwhile, forecasted cloudy sky with one or two spells of rain or thundershower in Kolkata and its adjoining areas.

"Thundershowers accompanied with lightning are likely in Kolkata and its adjoining areas because of the formation of convective activity and feeble system over the north-western Bay of Bengal," said L R Meena, deputy director-general, Alipore Meteorological Department.

According to Met department, the rains are caused by the retreating monsoon and they hope the weather will improve after 48 hours.

"Imagine, you are all dressed up to go out during Pujas but suddenly it starts raining," said Priyanka Mukherjee, a college student, fearing the rains might play spoilsport again.

Besides pandal hoppers, the pandal committees are also facing the brunt of nature.

"On Sasthi, our pandal was flooded by rains. It has now become muddy all over the place," said Bipradas Bhattacharya, secretary of the Vivekananda Sporting Club Puja committee, Haridevpur.

Heading: Nadia SP gets threat letter signed by Indian Mujahideen - Indian Express
Content:
Saptami marked the beginning of festive season in West Bengal, as people celebrated their favourite festival with fervour. What was new was the heightened security Kolkata had never witnessed before.

More than one crore people throng the city streets every day during the four days of the Pujas. In order to rule out any possibility of a terrorist attack on the city during the ongoing festival, the Kolkata police have beefed up security in and around the city. More than 20,000 policemen of Kolkata police have been pressed into service to man the entire city.

"Policemen have been deployed in every possible nook and corner of the city and in the pandals. Apart from men in uniform, plain-clothed security personnel will also be present throughout the city. Holidays and leaves have been cancelled," said a senior police officer of South division of Kolkata police.

Several big budget Pujas have been identified and special measures have been taken to prevent any threat to security. More policemen have been posted at the big budget puja pandals like Santosh Mitra Square, Mohammad Ali Park and College Square in North Kolkata and Ekdalia Park and Mudiali in South Kolkata.

Apart from the regular police forces who man the streets and manage crowds, special commandos trained to combat terrorist attacks have been deployed at these pandals since Sunday.

"Closed-circuit cameras have been put up at the big Pujas and the policemen will keep a close watch on the movements of the public from temporary control rooms set up near the pandals," said police commissioner Gautam Mohan Chakrabarti.

Although there is no specific threat perception or any specific information of terrorist attacks, the police have been put on high alert starting Monday, said a senior police officer of Lalbazar.

Many Puja committees have set up door-frame metal detectors at the entrance of their pandals to avoid untoward incidents. Volunteers from some of the Puja committees have been trained in security checking to provide a helping hand to the police.

"Some of these volunteers have been given hand held metal detectors and have been trained to use them," said a police officer.

On Saptami, meanwhile, lakhs of devotees spilled on the streets to seek the blessings of the Goddess. People from the suburbs started arriving in the city since afternoon. Those who wanted to avoid the crowd in the evening visited the pandals in the morning. The real flavour of the Pujas, however, became apparent only after the lights were on. The entire city was bathed in lights of different shapes and colours, and thousands gathered near the pandals only to view the splendour of illumination.

Police, however, said the rush on Saptami evening was not as much as they had expected. "The footfall here is about 5 to 7 thousand per hour. Last year it was much more," said a police officer posted at a big Puja pandal in South Kolkata. Police expect the number of people thronging the pandals to increase as the night deepens.

Heading: Kangra art adorns Howrah pandal - Indian Express
Content:
The superintendent of police of Nadia district received a threat letter in the name of Indian Mujahideen. Police, however, said the letter did not seem to be real.

Two days ago, the office of the Nadia SP received a letter in a sealed envelope. The entire administration went into a tizzy after the letter was opened by the secretary of the SP.

Though the police refused to divulge details of the letter, sources said the letter threatened that bombs would be placed and explosions would take place at various railway stations. The name of Indian Mujahideen was signed at the end of the letter.

Inspector General (Law and Order), Raj Kanojia, said the letter did not seem to be genuine. "The letter was posted locally from Chakdah post office. It said that bombs would be placed here and there," he said.

Keeping the festive rush in mind, however, the state administration did not take any chance and began immediate investigations apart from increasing security and checking. The GRP and the RPF were alerted and checking was intensified at important stations, including Howrah and Sealdah. Sniffer dogs were pressed into service at the stations.

Police, meanwhile, claimed that they have been able to identify the village from where the letter was sent. Earlier, in July, an e-mail in the name of the terrorist outfit was sent to a newspaper office, claiming that several vital installations would be blown up.

Heading: Clashes in Kumargunj over objectionable article outside Puja pandal - Indian Express
Content:
If you want to know about the Kangra Valley in Himachal Pradesh, all you need to do is step into one of the city pandals. As the Puja organisers are busy experimenting with a whole array of themes, Tarun Sporting Club in Howrah is showcasing Kangra art — an art form typical to Himachal Pradesh.

Reflecting the traditional Kangra art, the organisers have created replicas of an ancient wooden temple of the Kangra Valley and adorned it with Kangra style of painting in their pandal.

Six Kangra-style oil paintings on canvas, created especially for the pandal by Kangra artists, are on display outside the pandal. These paintings portray the images of Radha Krishna, for which Kangra art is famous.

"We have structured the pandal on the same lines as the age-old Radha Krishna temple in Kangra. We have replicated Kangra paintings of the 15-16th century, on canvas. All the paintings reveal the essence of Radha Krishna love story," said Kinshuk, artist and designer of the pandal.

The exterior of the pandal is designed to resemble the ancient wooden temple in Kangra. Wood being an expensive item of decoration, the committee members have used bamboo poles and polished it in a manner to give it the effect of real wood.

According to Kinshuk, the main idea behind the selection of the theme is to highlight one of the unique art forms of our country, which is not much popular among people.

To accentuate the temple-effect, a tulsi mancha is placed inside the pandal premises. Visitors entering the pandal are greeted at the entrance by two women, who welcome the visitors with Ganga water, trying to maintain the theme as much as possible. On entering the pandal, one would be drifted to a different ambience altogether, with the story of Radha Krishna etched on bamboos taking one to the divine settings of the Kangra valley.

To replicate the idols at the Kangra valley temple, the idols will be seen suspended in a three-dimensional way.

Heading: Truckloads of Hilsa arrives for Puja feast - Indian Express
Content:
Clashes broke out between police and an angry mob after an objectionable article was seen lying in front of a puja pandal at Kumargunj in North Dinajpur district on Monday.

The discovery of the article triggered tension in the area, following which people blocked road at two places. When police came to remove the blockade the protesters pelted stones at the police party. 15 policemen were injured in the clashes.

The police had to resort to firing after teargas and lathicharge failed to control the rampaging mob. Three rounds were fired by the police.

"So far 30 people have been arrested. Both the district magistrate and superintendent of police have received injuries. Personnel from BSF and RAF were immediately rushed to the spot to control the situation," Asok Mohan Chakrabarti, home secretary, said.

"I have asked the DM to call an all-party meeting today to resolve the crisis," the home secretary said. I also spoke to Minister for Jails and Social Welfare Biswanath Choudhury, who belongs to the district, regarding the issue, he added.

Heading: In the crowd of new pandals, city's oldest Puja stands out - Indian Express
Content:
There is good news for Hilsa-loving Bengalis. A record quantity of Hilsa from Bangladesh hit the Kolkata markets on Monday, just in time for the Puja feasts.

Forty truckloads of Hilsa reached Petrapol border in North 24 Parganas around 8 pm on Monday and were dispatched straight to the Sealdah wholesale market. Some early birds wanting to lap up the delicious fish had already queued up at the market when the trucks arrived.

According to traders, during Pujas there is an increase in the demand for the fish and there was a scarcity of Hilsa in the market for the last ten days. The wholesale prices were ranging between Rs 120 and Rs 140 kg this year.

Atul Das, president of the Hilsa Fresh Fish Importers Association, said: "We expect more fish to arrive in the next few days. The price in the retail market will range between Rs 180 and Rs 210. But the size of the fish is not large."

The association is also looking at the options of importing Hilsa cheaper.

"To import Hilsa from Myanmar, we need to pay 35 per cent import duty. We have appealed to the state Fisheries Department to waive the duty. If that happens, Hilsa will be available in the market at Rs 150 to Rs 200 per kg," Das said.

There is also speculation about the weight of Hilsa this year. Retail dealers claimed that the average weight of the fish was 700 to 900 grams, much less than the normal weight of 1,000 to 1,200 grams.

Traders added that if the duty is waived, not just Hilsa, but other fish like Katla, Rohu and Mrigel can also be imported.

For healthy Pujas
The Apollo Gleneagles Hospital will set up health booths at six of the biggest pandals in the city at College Square, Mohammad Ali Park, Santosh Mitra Square, Kaizer St Complex, Telenga Bagan and Gariahat Circle. The group will also post ambulances near four major pandals at Topsia PS, Tollygunge PS, Lake PS and DC ND Office.

Heading: Optical illusion: see this pandal from a distance - Indian Express
Content:
Every year during Durga Puja, several new pandals mushroom in almost all the localities of Kolkata.

The charm of the old Pujas in the city, however, remains intact and not threatened by the newer ones.

One such Puja that has managed to survive over centuries, and yet retain its old-world charm, is Behala's Sabarna Roy Chowdhuri Aathchala Bari — the oldest Durga Puja in West Bengal.

Celebrated in the city since 1610, the puja was first organised by Lakhshmi Kant Majumder, the then head of the family. Centuries have passed since then, and the family has had numerous heads.

But the essence of the Puja remains the same.

This year, celebrating 399 years of their historical Puja, the Sabarna family is celebrating seven Durga pujas —- six at Barisha (Aathchala Bari, Baro Bari, Mejo Bari, Benaki Bari, Kalikingkar Bhavan and Majher Bari) and another at Birati.

The family claims they don't believe in any theme, and prefer maintaining their traditional way of performing Puja.

The Sabarna family gives the traditional look of Bhakti Trangini Durga to their idol, and built their pandal in a simple, traditional way.

Subhash Roy Chowdhury, one of the family members, said: "I am the 33rd generation member of the family, which is celebrating the oldest Durga Puja in Kolkata. We are following the old principles followed by our ancestors for performing the Puja."

He added, "It is like a chain system, in which the next generation follows the traditions of the previous generation." The family members come together to contribute funds for organising the puja, and sponsors or advertisers are not allowed in their pandal.

Heading: Walk-in to have a feel of Maya, Inca civilizations - Indian Express
Content:
Being one of the most attractive destinations among pandal hoppers in north Kolkata, the Puja pandal at Nalin Sarkar Street is famous for the uniqueness of its idea conceptualised by noted artist Sanatan Dinda.

According to the committee, they have created the country's highest artistic illusion this year — a ten-and-a-half-feet structure — which looks abstract up front, but one can make out exactly what the picture conveys only from a distance.

Dinda might have given the Puja pandals a miss this year, but the Nalin Sarkar Street Puja committee has made sure that their pandal remains a top draw even this year.

"The highest illusion is probably at Science City and another one is at Kanpur, but none is as high as ours," said Samak Saha, secretary of the Puja committee. The centre of the pandal has the goddess Durga painted on flex rolls, while walls have images of Brahma, Vishnu, Maheshwara and Hara Parvati. The entrance to the pandal is through a structure that gives the illusion of entering the mouth of Mahisasura. "Our idea is to make people feel that they have entered the body of the slained asura to see the goddess," Saha said.

Heading: Roll over Barreto - Indian Express
Content:
Two of the world's most mysterious civilizations, Maya and Inca, have found their way to a pandal in north Kolkata this Puja. The organisers of the Lake Town Netaji Sporting Club Puja have left no stone unturned to create an authentic Mayan village in the grounds of the club.

"The idea is to bring these civilizations to life. I have researched for months on their culture and most of the artifacts that adorn the pandal are the replicas of the original ones," said Sanjit Ghosh, the brain behind the concept.

"Worshipping nature is common to both these civilization and it the main theme of our Puja," Ghosh added.

An Inca burial ground has been recreated in the pandal to focus on the Incan preoccupation with death and rebirth.

"The cycle of life was very important for this civilization. We hope to draw parallels with some of our indigenous beliefs with their rituals," he said.

Artificial bonfires will be lit around the pandal to impart an authentic Mayan village look to it. "We also plan to source tribal songs of these civilisations from south America," Ghosh said.

For Ghosh, cinematic aspects of the village are important. "I want the pandal to be a complete audio-visual experience for visitors. When we think of a civilization we think of its people, their music and rituals. The music that we will play in the pandal will be in keeping with the mood," he said.

Being associated with the world of cinema has helped Ghosh in this endeavour. "I have worked as an art director in a number of South Indian productions. This Puja happens to be a dream project for me," he said.

Nearly 40 artisans were involved in the construction of the pandal. "It took us nearly two months to complete the pandal. Although most of the structures are made of plaster of paris, we have also used clay and wood to make idols," he added.

Ghosh said when visitors would walk into the pandal they would get transported to the rainforests of South America.

"Visitors will walk out of the pandal with knowledge of two different cultures, besides having an aesthetically pleasing experience," he said.

Heading: Sahara injects big money into Bengal hockey - Indian Express
Content:
The Brazilian's performance in the first two matches of the I-League gives ample evidence that he is past his prime

Amal Dutta had set the cat among the pigeons. He lost his job, but he was right on the money.

A couple of seasons ago, when Dutta was in charge of Mohun Bagan, he had questioned an aging Barreto's ability to be successful at the national level. His comments hadn't gone down well with the Bagan management and the veteran coach eventually lost his job.

The officials continue to put faith in the Brazilian who helped his team win back-to-back Kolkata league titles. But as things get tougher at the national level, he took a backseat.

The first two matches of this I-League gave ample evidence that Barreto has become too slow to be effective. Time for the pink slip?

A former India international, who as a coach has won the National League and the Federation Cup, concurs. "Barreto is a spent force. Experience makes up for his lack of fitness in the local league. But in the I-League, he is no longer a match-winner," he said on condition of anonymity.

"He is struggling to get into the right position. He is taking an awful lot of time to turn and take a crack at the goal. He is past his prime. Make no mistake, he is one of the best foreigners ever to play in India. But now he has become a liability," he added.

Former East Bengal coach Manoranjan Bhattacharya, however, prefers to wait and watch. He has played only two matches in this I-League. So, I think it's a little too premature to jump into a conclusion. He barely had any rest after a grueling Kolkata league.

"It takes some time to recover and get back to full fitness. We should wait till the first phase of the tournament is over," Bhattacharya opined.

His observations raised a pertinent question. Why do the Kolkata clubs give so much importance to a "meaningless tournament"?

National coach Bob Houghton has time and again said that the local league should be supportive to the I-League, not a competitor. Youngsters, rather than the old guards should play in the state leagues. His suggestions so far have fallen on deaf ears.

Club officials have their excuses ready. "As because we are the fan-based clubs, we can't ignore the local league."

They refuse to look at the bigger picture.

Heading: Anand gears up for battle of nerves with Kramnik - Indian Express
Content:
BHA invites Pakistani team for indoor tournament this November

In a heartening development for the beleaguered Bengal hockey circuit, the sponsors of the popular Premier Hockey League (PHL) — Sahara India Pariwar — have announced to pump in nearly Rs 70 lakh for a four-year period in the state. Confirming this development, Bengal Hockey Association (BHA) treasurer Gopinath Ghosh said that the aim of the fresh injection of cash has come about as an initiative from BHA president JB Roy. "Basically, the sponsors have decided to do something for Bengal hockey, to promote and revive the game in areas that matter. They will inject Rs 17.5 lakh every year now, for a four-year period. Such amount being poured into Bengal hockey is unprecedented," Ghosh said.

Meanwhile, the BHA is inviting a team from Pakistan this November to take part in a six-a-side indoor hockey that will be played at the Netaji Indoor Stadium. Bengal and the Pakistani team apart, the other participants are teams from Chennai, Delhi, Punjab, Mumbai, Karnataka and Indian Airlines.

The prestigious Beighton Cup this year has been slated for December 12 to 22, and it will be played at SAI's Kolkata complex. The BHA is eagerly waiting for the monsoon to get over soon so that the Astroturf, which is safely tucked away, can be laid out on time for the Beighton Cup. However, if the SAI authorities fail to set up the Astroturf in time, the tournament would then be played on grass, the BHA treasurer informed.

The following are the office-bearers elected at the BHA's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on Saturday.

President: JB Roy, Vice-Presidents: Surajit Purkayastha, Kumaresh Sen, Utpal Ganguly, Noomi Mehta, Russi Jeejeebhoy, Secretary: Gurbax Singh, Treasurer: Gopinath Ghosh.

Heading: Dalal wins Rolon racing championship - Indian Express
Content:
Viswanathan Anand says his upcoming World Championship match against Russia's Vladimir Kramnik would be a battle of nerves because his opponent is as well prepared as he is for the showpiece event.

Anand, who is giving undivided attention to his match preparation since April, will defend his World Champion title against Kramnik in Bonn, Germany from October 11.

"Well, it's a challenge you have to enjoy it and give it your best. I have prepared well. I guess there is no better way to answer this question," Anand said.

"I have done both, a physical regimen as well as extensive work. Since it's a 12-game match, keeping the nerves till the end will be very important. Stamina and mental fitness will also be something I will be working on," he said. Anand added he also took care to relax during tournaments.

"I generally try and relax during tournaments also by watching movies, going to the gym or just taking a long walk. Now I'm just getting ready for the match," he said.

The 38-year-old Indian ace, who slipped out of the FIDE's top-3 after more than a decade in the latest rankings earlier this month, was not unduly bothered about the dip and said he was focusing on match preparation than anything else.

"If you see, on January 1 both Kramnik and myself were No 1 in the world. We can then see that we have spent the rest of the year just training for each other," said Anand, who slid to the fifth spot.

Having said that, Anand insisted he did not repent playing in the Chess Masters Final in Bilbao, which cost him precious rating points and the top ranking.

"At Linares, I was able to play well and win and in Wijk (Aan Zee-Corus Championships) make a very strong comeback to get the third place. But since April the focus has clearly been the (World Championship) match.

"When I went to Bilbao I was quite clear that I wouldn't be in the best of form as I have not really been working on my immediate rivals but rather on one person. So I don't repent having played there," he said.

Anand agreed Kramnik was more comfortable in match-plays than the tournament but predicted that the matches would be well fought and hold public interest.

"He (Kramnik) is a very classical player and has a very deep understanding of chess. He feels very comfortable in matches. Since we do a lot of work and especially now a days with computers, both of us will have an extensive analysis."

Heading: Reel Devi - Indian Express
Content:
Gaurav Dalal clinched the title in the premium Formula Rolon category with a series of spectacular performance in the current season. The curtains came down on a season which saw several upsets and fluctuating fortunes as the lead changed hands several times. However, once Gaurav got the lead, he held on to it and consolidated his position through consistent performances and eventually won the championship. Saran Vikram of Wallace Sports had earlier annexed the title in the Formula Swift category.

The season also witnessed tremendous rivalry between the veterans and the pugnacious youngsters. Delighted were the weekend crowd who turned up to witness the races for one final time this season.

From the saloon cars to the Super Bikes to the Formula racing cars, it was a blend of exhilarating speed and excellent driving skills with the cream of Indian racers exhibiting their skills.

Heading: Divinity at a Distance - Indian Express
Content:
War not over for Buddha, State has a slew of ambitious projects up its sleeves

When Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee recently said that though he had lost a battle in Singur, but his war for industrialisation was still on, he was not making a statement that was political alone.

For, Bhattacharjee's confidence stems from dozens of projects worth thousands of crores of rupees, which are either in the pipeline or have already been implemented over the last decade.

From 1991 to 2007, the state has seen the implementation of 1,729 large and medium projects with a total investment of Rs 37,805 crore. In 2007 alone, 291 industrial projects worth Rs 5,073 crore were implemented.

At least nine large-scale integrated steel manufacturing projects are in the pipeline. Leading the pack is the Sajjan Jindal group-promoted 5,000 acre, Rs 35,000 crore, 10 million tonne capacity steel plant in Maoist-affected Salboni belt of West Midnapore.

Besides, there are proposed plants for chemicals, petrochemicals, paper, tyres, wagon-making, ship building and oil refineries. Add to this, are a slew of industrial parks catering to specific sectors like leather, jewellery, garments, plastic, bio-tech and IT/ITES.

Heading: HUDA takes garbage site to villages, draws ire - Indian Express
Content:
These days, the probasi Bengali does not fret if he cannot be in Kolkata for pujo. Neither does he necessarily want to. While the zealous charm of visiting a puja pandal down every block can only be experienced in Bengal, Bengalis in different part of the world celebrate Maa Durga's homecoming in their own distinctive styles. A probasi Bengali tells us what puja means in their corners of the world

The holy month of Ramadan is over. The Eid celebrations have just ended. People are back to work, but for a small community of Dubai, it is celebration time. As the relentless Dubai summer melts to a more tolerable winter, the small but boisterous population of Bengalis in the city are all geared up for Durga Puja .

The Sindhi community hall which is generally used by the Bengali association of Dubai for Durga Puja celebrations, is the bastion of the teenaged volunteers of the community, who happily stay up late in the night, decorating the hall with festoons and streamers . The housewives play an important role in the festivities as they willingly take up a number of responsibilities.

The Bhog an essential part of the festivities, is lovingly prepared by a Brahmin woman of the community, and every year there are a number of them eagerly awaiting their turn to display their culinary skills. The purohit (usually a family relative of one of the members of the community) arrives from Kolkata, the lists of the puja essentials are faxed or emailed well in advance. Some essential items are bought by the purohit himself.

The small six inches statutes reminds us of a child's dollset, but her diminished stature does not diminish the devotion of her followers.

Mahastami is the day when most Bengalis try to make it to the hall for the maha pushpanjali, office and school notwithstanding. Held according to the Indian timings, the puspanjali is a crowded affair. The women, decked in their finest sarees and jewellery are a sight to behold. The men, howling children in tow, take on the responsibility of handling the children while their better halves socialise before offering prayers to the goddess.

The sindoor khela is another occasion which the Bengali women of the city don't miss, clad in trademark red-bordered sarees, try and recreate the fervour of the festivities backhome. By Dashami evening, a pall of gloom descends upon the hall as the bhashan procession is carried out quietly in the dark, as immersion of clay idols is illegal in Dubai. Instead of the muddy waters of Ganga, our beloved Maa is immersed in the turquoise blue Arabian Sea.

The Bongo Parishad members hold a bijayasamelani at the posh confines of a five-star hotel, where kurta and saree clad members gather to plan the next year's festivities.

Heading: Rs 47-lakh makeover for Khan Market - Indian Express
Content:
To protest against the decision of the authorities to shift a landfill site from near DLF Phase I to Bandwari village, nearly 100 villagers blocked the Faridabad-Gurgaon Road on Monday morning for around 15 minutes.

The villagers alleged that if the site was shifted to the new location, it would create serious problem for over 40 villages in Gurgaon, Faridabad and Delhi. Most of these villages fall within the one-km radius of the proposed dumping site. "One can imagine the kind of garbage cities produce. If the landfill site of Gurgaon and Faridabad is shifted here, it would not only produce unbearable stench but would also irreparably pollute our land and water," said Antaram Kanwal, a resident of Tigra village. The panchayat has decided not to accept the compensation offered by HUDA for the site, he added.

Senior police officers seemed unaware of the situation. DCP (east) Jagdish Nagar said: "I have no information that the road was blocked."

An official said HUDA had obtained a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Centre for shifting the site. "Before any such plan is carried out, there is a public hearing, after which an NOC is provided. HUDA has prepared a detailed project report about treating the waste before the garbage is disposed," he said. Municipal Corporation of Faridabad and Gurgaon will rope in a private agency to ensure that the waste is treated before its disposal, he said.

Heading: Baggage delay: Lufthansa asked to pay up Rs 2.5 lakh - Indian Express
Content:
Khan Market's trendy shops, gourmet restaurants, boutique-like atmosphere and spot-on location have made it one of the costliest pieces of commercial real estate in the Capital. To preserve its status as a favoured shopping destination of VIPs, diplomats and foreign tourists, an effort is now on to spruce up the market.

"The ongoing construction of a boundary wall along with development of the footpath is to cost around Rs 20 lakh, and is likely to be competed by the end of this month," Anand Kumar Tiwari, NDMC public relations director, said. The fancy boundary wall, with a decorative iron grill and the new footpath around it, will give a new look to the market, particularly if one is approaching it from Subramania Bharti Marg.

The current beautification drive is part of a plan formulated by the NDMC in consultation with shopkeepers in 2003-04.The plan, with an estimated budget of Rs 47 lakh, also involves the development of parking lots in the market. A parking lot has come up on what was once a disused park at the back of the market, complete with water harvesting pits, a piao and hydrants for the horticulture department to maintain the greenery with. The inner service lane dividing the two buildings of the market has been paved with designer bricks. Another parking lot has come up in front of Lok Nayak Bhavan.

In a first of its kind, the market has appointed a number of parking attendants, who are supposed to act as local traffic wardens apart from helping shoppers park their cars safely. Strategically placed boards announce that they are not to be paid anything.

Most shopkeepers are for the beautification drive. Balraj Bahri of Bahri Sons said: "It is good for the market and for the shoppers as well."

Sanjeev Mehra, president of the Khan Market Traders' Association, while applauding the beautification effort, said it had taken too long and should have been taken up in one go. "By the time one part is complete, the other begins to wear out," he said.

The NDMC is also trying to tackle complaints of power outages and overloading in the market. At present, the market receives a supply of 5,000 KVA from the substation at Lok Nayak

Bhavan. Some of the extra demand is being met from the adjoining substation at Golf Apartments with a supply of 2,000 KVA.

Heading: Time to say good-bye - Indian Express
Content:
German airlines Lufthansa have been directed by the State Consumer Commission to pay Rs 2.5 lakh as compensation to a city businessman for delayed delivery of baggage containing his business orders.

In its order last month the Commission held the airlines guilty of "deficiency in service" as the complainant, Ajay Khanna, who was returning from London, had to cancel a business deal. According to the complainant, the purchaser served him a legal notice for failure to deliver the product on time.

"The circumstance of delay in delivering baggage itself amounts to deficiency in service for which (a) consumer is entitled for compensation," Commission president Justice J D Kapoor ruled.

According to the complaint, Khanna went to Europe on a business trip in October 1999 and took a Lufthansa flight back from London. At the airport in London, the authorities checked his baggage containing business orders worth over £14,000 and attached a tag number to it as per norm. But on reaching Delhi, Khanna told the consumer commission, the luggage with the tag number was not his.

He then informed the Lufthansa office — both here and in Frankfurt.

Eighteen days after the incident, Khanna's baggage was finally delivered, though in a "highly pilfered condition". The airlines accepted the delay but denied any negligence on its part. It also cited provisions under the Carrier Act to contend that Khanna was only entitled to compensation at the rate of US$ 20 per kilogram.

The airlines later sent him a cheque worth Rs 9,167 and a discounted ticket to the US as compensation. Khanna then approached the consumer panel, seeking a compensation of Rs 17 lakh.

The airlines argued before the Commission that though there had been delay, the baggage was later delivered in good condition.

Justice Kapoor however, held Lufthansa's services to be "deficient, resulting in unnecessary mental harassment, loss of business and agony of the consumer".

Heading: Indian judokas gearing up for junior world meet - Indian Express
Content:
Federation ratifies new rules, does away with longer format for billiards national championship in Indore

The Billiards and Snooker Federation of India (BSFI) has finally decided to do away with the time format in billiards to make it as attractive as snooker. The decision was voted upon by member units at the Kolkata AGM last week and will come into effect during the Senior National Championships to be held at Indore from November 8.

Confirming the decision, BSFI vice-president Ravi K Tandon told Sportline that the national federation was left with no choice but to introduce the change after pressure from all quarters. "We also had to think of our medal prospects in the Asian Games in Guangzhou (China) in 2010," said Tandon.

The new format would mean the game will be played in 150-frame up, with best of five to start with up to the quarter-finals. The semi-finals will be played as best of seven frames while the final will be of best of 11 frames.

The BSFI has also introduced qualifiers to help those who do not get entries directly from the state units make the grade. "This will help players get entry into the main round. The qualifiers, up to the group matches, will be played in 100-up frames with best of five games," Tandon said.

He admitted there were pressures from players as well as sponsors to do away with the much-longer time format but added that since the Asian body has adopted this format, it was the logical step to introduce it at the national championships to give "our players sufficient practice."

Tandon also said that Indians had an advantage at major events in the new format since they are used to big breaks, citing the recent World Championships in Bangalore as an example. "We had all the semi-finalists from India. That's an indication of how well our players have adapted themselves to the format," he said.

However, on the flip side, there will hardly be any time for the players to relax because a good player with great concentration can finish the frame on a single visit. "So no player can relax and expect his opponent to commit mistakes. He may not get his chance at all."

Besides, the longer version of billiards was not viewer-friendly and had failed to attract sponsors as well. "Despite having 14 world champions in the game, we were struggling to get sponsors. We had to do a lot of convincing before somebody reluctantly agreed. But there are several takers for the new version," he said.

Heading: Memories of A Melancholic Soul - Indian Express
Content:
Too much crowd, too much madness and too little faith push quite a few people away from the giant circus that is Durga Puja in Kolkata today

If we assume that the drone of the dhak in the nearby Puja pandal, the confusing flavours of the mix of khichudi, payash and labda in a earthen cup, and the sweaty crowd dressed in crisp new clothes clicking pictures of the goddess, make the day for any Bengali of the faith, it would be an audacious generalisation. Because, the Durga Puja that is today, have a lot of our clan thinking otherwise. Anirban Ghosh, a second year student of mass communication and videography at the St Xavier's College, suffers from mild claustrophobia. "It's not all that serious otherwise but these pandals filled to their capacity make me feel very uncomfortable," says Ghosh.

Add to that the music, the din, the organizers shouting out instructions over the microphone, the Pujas, for the likes of Ghosh can turn out to be quite disappointing. Ditto for Bishwakshen Bandyopadhyay. The research student at Hyderabad Central University, finds today's Puja too blinding, too flashy for his taste. Reason why he tries staying away from the 'indulgence'. "The Pujas these days are neither ritualistic or spiritual, nor do they give you a feeling of home. It's too plastic for my taste," says Bandyopadhyay, whose parents too refrain from the festivities because their son keeps away from them.

"Any celebration, at the end of the day, is about feeling good. I guess my parents don't feel greater than usual, during the Pujas because I don't. Their feelings are naturally very closely aligned to mine," smiles Bandyopadhyay.

The contemporary idiom of the Pujas in Kolkata pushes several away from the festivities. Like Tapati Talukdar, a housewife. "There's too much crowd, too much sound and madness around," says Talukdar, who used to celebrate the Pujas in her home as a child. "The Pujas these days feel very distant. There are TV channels, radio channels, corporate giants - all running competitions etc. It all looks like a circus," says Talukdar. What with the security checks, the serpentine queues that move at snail's pace and a whole fetish for crowd count, the likes of Talukdar have little charm left in the Pujas.

Veer Sen, a retired professional, says that despite their being Brahmo, Pujas have very important implications in their life. "It is a time when we do what we love doing – travel that is," says Sen. Sen hunts out places which is not frequented by the usual revelers and usually goes on a long drive. "The chaos of the Pujas in the city, the publicity blitzkrieg, are a little unnerving," says Sen.

Heading: Full Circle - Indian Express
Content:
Rita Ganguly remembers Begum Akhtar not only as ghazal legend but also as a successful woman of the early 20th century

Rita Ganguly sits gracefully in spite of the heat when we meet at the Terrace Café at Triveni Kala Sangam. Further, she shows no sign of hurrying up our chat for her afternoon flight to Mumbai, for the launch of her book on Begum Akhtar. When I ask for her favourite Akhtar anecdote, she laughs: "There are so many stories about Ammi. But what I remember most is one night in 1966 when she went over to my guru and thumri legend Siddheshwari Devi, ending their 32-year-old feud, and asked her for a favour — to let me join her as a disciple." Ganguly is arguably Akhtar's last chosen disciple and after years of hearing many stories about her teacher, she is determined to set the record straight.

Ae Mohabbat: Reminiscing Begum Akhtar (Stellar Publishers, Rs 695) delves into the life and times of Akhtaribai Faizabadi, better known as Begum Akthar. Ganguly writes about an enthusiastic young singer from north India who burst into the scene in the late 1920s and soon became the darling of the music world. "She juggled her multiple roles as a performer, lover, wife, mother, guru and friend," says Ganguly. "But beneath the facade of fame, she was a deeply sensitive woman, facing loneliness, pain and anguish," she adds solemnly.

Ganguly began her research into Akhtar's life in 2000, when, on a Ford Foundation Fellowship, she documented the lives of tawaifs as a musical community, searching for a comprehensive repertoire of their music and, finally, recording over 200 hours of rare music. "Ammi has mistakenly been branded as a tawaif and a thief for decades now. In music circles, women have always been mistreated, misinterpreted. I wanted to write the story of her life from the perspective of a successful, working woman, much ahead of her times," says Ganguly, who in 2002, wrote and performed a solo play called Begum Akhtar and toured extensively with it. The book is as much about Akthar as it is about the emergence of classical music in post-Independence India.

Ganguly's sure that quite a few feathers will be ruffled, "So many of her disciples even claim that I wasn't her student. That's all right. It only lessens the burden of her legacy and allows me to record in whatever genre I want," chuckles Ganguly, who is releasing a thumri album later this month. "Ammi's greatest lesson to me was life, and how to look at it. She used to say, if you want to achieve anything in life, then make friends with loneliness, it won't betray you."

Heading: Lap it Up - Indian Express
Content:
Mugdha Godse on moving from the real world of fashion to Madhur Bhandarkar's reel version of it

She had strutted the ramp and faced enough flashbulbs, but did not quite realise how nerve-wracking it would be to act it all out — until she faced Madhur Bhandarkar for her first shot for Fashion. The dusky Mugdha Godse is now happy about her role as a failed model, as Bhandarkar ponders on the seamy side of the extravaganza we see on the runway.

Dressed in a black singlet and denims, her minimalistic look a sharp contrast to her glam avatar on screen, the 23-year-old confesses to exhaustion, as she juggles ad shoots, promotions and dubbing. "I am so excited — and nervous. Ever since the promos started on the TV, the expectations have gone up though the enormity of the situation has yet to sink in," she says.

In the movie to be released around Diwali, Godse plays Janet Sequeira, alongside Priyanka Chopra, Kangana Ranaut and Arbaaz Khan. "The movie is about the emotional journey of models at different stages of their careers and Madhur has captured it aptly," she says. Between posing for photographs, she says she had no inkling she could act. Hers has been the typical small-town-girl story. "I studied in a Marathi-medium school in Pune. It was in college that I understood the basics of grooming," she says. Her ambition drove her to the sequined universe of fashion. Then at an ad shoot, Bhandarkar spotted her and offered the part in Fashion — and Bollywood easily became part of her resume.

It was after Godse signed the film that the grill began. She attended a crash course in acting at Anupam Kher's school and took Kathak lessons, which she claims helped her synchronise expressions, movements and feelings. Recounting her first time in front of the camera, she boasts at having given her first shot in just two takes. "And once the shot was okayed, everybody applauded. I can still hear the sound of those claps," she adds.

The Bollywood bug has bitten and the debutante is clearly not keen on continuing her old life as a model — she has cut down her ad assignments and has been attending script-reading sessions. Her three-movie deal with Percept is also in the pipeline, but there is one more bow on the runway. "You will see me at the forthcoming Lakme Fashion Week ... this time as a show stopper," she laughs.

Heading: Brawn Power - Indian Express
Content:
Nikki Duggal detests the usual black laptop bags. Then she got creative with her loathing and came up with Woccow, a brand-new range of laptop bags that are to hit stores just in time for Diwali.

Duggal, a 31-year-old Delhi-based designer who runs Nikki Duggal Design as well as Mixed Juice Design studio, does all her work on her laptop and so the bag is more than an accessory for her, it is an extension of her style statement. "The black bags that you get with most laptops are boring, so I thought I would make my own laptop bag," says Duggal, who began working on it four months ago.

Inspiring the covers is not anything remotely related to the computer; instead it is the sacred cow. And the word "cow" appears twice, once in reverse, in the brand name Woccow, creating a whacky, retro effect. "I want to celebrate the image," says Duggal, who has the signature cow on the base of the bags which are available in a variety of colours, from raven-black with neon-pink stripes to beige and white. Made of felt, nylon and faux leather, the bags are lightweight and equipped with thin, sturdy straps that allow you to loop your arm through them or carry them like a briefcase.

But be prepared to dig deep into your pockets for one of these. Priced between Rs 5,000 and Rs 6,500, the bags come with one-year guarantee. If you can't wait for these to hit the stores, drop by at her studio and bag them.

For details contact, 40545035

Heading: Post-Wall Ball - Indian Express
Content:
When Ashoo Sharma enters an akhara, it is to shoot, not wrestle

It is an innocent curtained door that leads into the akhara — a darkened courtyard and a very different world. One that is divided into a series of raised platforms, where musclemen caked in mud lock each other in a deathly embrace and nobody wants to blink first. In this formidable world of the akhara, which changes scrawny village boys into men with iron triceps, photographer Ashoo Sharma's Nikon camera has been romancing sweat-stained fighters as they prepare for supremacy.
