Commenting on the political developments, Ambika Soni said the Congress high command was keeping a close eye on the statements of Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee spokesperson and former MLA Bir Devinder Singh. She said PPCC chief Mohinder Singh Kaypee would provide them a report and the party was not bothered about what Bir writes in his book. She also announced that the UPA government would soon make public the report related to financial and developmental schemes in Punjab and there was no discrimination with the SAD-BJP government. She said even Punjab Finance Minister Manpreet Badal praised the Centre for economic assistance.

Heading: 5,000 Ramlilas keep police on toes - Indian Express
Content:
As part of the celebrations of the Chandigarh Heritage Festival, UT Administrator General S F Rodrigues (Retd) flagged off a heritage walk from the Open Hand Monument to the Chandigarh War Memorial in Leisure Valley on Tuesday.

The event, sponsored by the State Bank of India and marked with the spirit of sportsmanship and enthusiasm, attracted a huge participation of people from different walks of life including social activists, sportspersons, senior citizens, environmentalists and students. General Rodrigues, along with the participants, joined the walk and talked about the strategies to preserve the city's heritage.

He emphasised on the need to make the heritage walk a regular feature. "Such occasions motivate our children and young people in nation-building activities and inculcate in them a sense of faith and confidence to move ahead," he said.

Sharing his vision with the architects and senior citizens associated with maintaining the city, General Rodrigues called for active partnership to restore the grandeur of Chandigarh. "It is not solely the responsibility of the government agencies but, as concerned citizens, we must actively join the endeavour and promote our culture and glorious traditions," he said.

Rajnish Vatts, principal, Chandigarh College of Architecture, explained the concept of Capitol Complex and the philosophy and vision of Le Corbusier in designing different important buildings in the city. Besides senior officers from the Chandigarh Administration including Home Secretary Ram Niwas, Tourism Director Vivek Atray, top functionaries of the State Bank of India including Ajay Swaroop, Chief General Manager, Chandigarh Circle, V Murli, General Manager-1 and A K Gupta, General Manager-2, were present on the occasion.

Heading: FM’s statement not view of govt: Minister - Indian Express
Content:
At a time when the sound of bomb blasts is resonating in the country, over 5,000 Ramlilas across the state have sent the Punjab Police in a tizzy.

Sources said in a recent meeting, Punjab DGP NPS Aulakh had issued instructions to officers, especially SSPs, to provide adequate security cover during the festival season. Majority of the personnel of the 70,000-strong force are already on law and order duty from 8 pm to midnight, the time when Ramlilas are held.

Of the 5,000 Ramlilas, 2,500 are held in Majha, 1,000 in Doaba and rest in Malwa. However, there are only 150 registered Ramlila Societies in Majha.

About 10 policemen are deployed at each site, which is inadequate. Besides, people are not being frisked and parking space has been kept close to the Ramlila ground or on the road.

"Each district has a dog squad, but it is pressed into VIP service the moment they arrive. Force has also been deployed in the markets and other busy places and more nakas have been set up," said a police official. Sources said force of this magnitude had never been deployed in Punjab.

Talking to The Indian Express, IGP (Jalandhar Zone) Sanjeev Kalra said, "In Jalandhar city alone, about 60 Ramlilas are going on. We have made adequate security arrangements and even deployed the staff working in the offices of the officers. On our request, the temple managements have deployed private security and installed CCTVs."

Sources said during the interrogation of Harjant Singh, a militant who was recently arrested by the Jalandhar Police with a pistol and two magazines, it came to light that the migrant labourers from Bihar were on his targets and he had chosen busy market places during the festival season to execute his nefarious designs.

Heading: Longevity equals loneliness, finds GMCH study - Indian Express
Content:
Finance Minister Manpreet Badal got little support from his cabinet colleague and Transport Minister Master Mohan Lal on the issue of subsidies.

Mohan Lal said the recent statement on subsidies could not be taken as an opinion of the government. The senior BJP leader said the SAD-BJP combine fought the elections on this plank and the views of the Finance Minister were his own.

Mohan Lal said this during an interaction after the installation of Harjit Singh Grewal of the BJP as the chairman of the Punjab Information and Communication Technology Corporation Limited (Punjab Infotech) today.

When asked how the BJP took the CM's warning to all cabinet colleagues, Mohan Lal said Manpreet's statement could be discussed in the cabinet meeting.

The Transport Minister said 100 AC buses would start plying from November 1, and these include 50 buses of the Punjab Roadways and another 50 of the Punsub. These would be ordinary AC buses, he said.

Heading: 20 hurt as three cars, auto collide - Indian Express
Content:
Study states 72.8 per cent women suffer from loneliness as compared to 65.6 per cent men

In the dusk of their lives, it seems that the elderly in the city sorely miss a supporting hand.

And in an ironic twist, it's the women who feel lonelier than men owing to their higher life expectancy.

A recent study conducted by Department of Community Medicine, Government Medical College and Hospital in Sector 32, found that 72.8 per cent of females suffer from loneliness as compared to 65.6 per cent males.

Published in the Indian Journal of Community Medicine, the study surveyed 361 individuals (152 males, 209 females) in the age group of 65 to 92 years in Chandigarh.

Longevity was stated as the primary reason behind loneliness as the study found that those living with their spouse fared better on the loneliness scale.

"Contributory factors for higher loneliness in females were loss of companion, illiteracy, less social contacts and maltreatment by family members," notes the study.

Also, the study found that loneliness was more prevalent among persons who lived alone (92.2 per cent) as compared to those living with their spouse (58.9per cent) or family (61.4per cent).

It was higher among widows (85.2 per cent) and widowers (75.8 per cent) who lived with the family as compared to those sharing house with a spouse (58.9 per cent).

Also, it is not just loneliness affecting elderly women but also other ailments as well. Incidence of illness was higher in females (59.5 per cent) than males (40.5 per cent).

Hypertension was the most common problem with 46 per cent of women and 34 per cent of men suffering from it.

Heading: Ranjit Singh’s bust auctioned for 1.1 lakh pounds - Indian Express
Content:
Vehicles stranded on NH-21 for over 3 hours

Twenty persons were injured after three cars and an autorickshaw collided on the Kharar-Ropar stretch of National Highway-21 near Sahoran village, about 3 kilometres from Kharar, on Tuesday evening.

The accident disrupted traffic on the busy highway and long queues of cars extended on both sides of the road for over three hours.

Five of the injured — Hashwinder Singh of Lakhnaur, Avtar Singh from Nayagaon, Urmila Devi, Suraj Gir from Anandpur Sahib and Rajiv Kapila — were admitted to Government Medical College and Hospital, Sector 32, Chandigarh.

They were stated to be in a serious condition. Rano and Navjeet from Burail were admitted in the Kharar Civil Hospital.

The remaining were discharged from hospital after treatment.

Sources said the accident occurred around 6 pm when four vehicles, moving in different directions, collided while overtaking each other.

Investigating Officer Malkiat Singh refused to comment despite repeated efforts.

Heading: One held for sexual harassment - Indian Express
Content:
A 19th Century stunning marble bust of Maharajah Ranjit Singh, the erstwhile ruler of Punjab, was auctioned for 1,10,400 pounds at Bonhams Indian and Islamic Sale. The bust sculpted in India was estimated to sell for about 50,000 pounds to 70,000 pounds at Bonhams, one of the oldest and largest auctioneers of art in the world.

Clare Penhallurick, head of Indian and Islamic Art at Bonhams, said "We are delighted to offer this magnificent sculpture for sale, particularly as last year we sold a bust of Ranjit Singh's son, Duleep Singh, for 1.7 million pounds."

Ranjit Singh had built an empire which stretched from the Indian Ocean to the Himalayas and he is revered by Sikhs as the last effective ruler of independent Punjab. Within 10 years of his death, his empire was in the hands of East India Company and many of his treasures, including the priceless Kohinoor diamond, had become Queen Victoria's property.

Heading: Dentist to cough up Rs 30,000 for faulty treatment - Indian Express
Content:
The Tarn Taran police arrested Gurvail Singh of Sur Singh village in Tarn Taran for allegedly attempting to sexually assault a minor girl. Sources said the accused and his brother, Ram Singh, ran a chemist shop in the village and offered money to the victim and her sister, also a minor, for sexual favours.

They said the victim and her sister worked as housemaids and Gurvail Singh had tried to assault them when they were returning home from work.

Sources said the accused had thrashed the girls and their mother when she came to rescue them.

Heading: Amarinder asks Badal to come clean on ‘missing land records’ - Indian Express
Content:
The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum has directed a city-based dentist to pay Rs 15,000 as compensation and refund Rs 15,750 charged as fee for deficiency in services.

Dr Sandeep Verma, who runs a clinic in Sector 20, Chandigarh, has been asked to refund the amount within 30 days, failing which he will be liable to pay a penal interest at the rate of 12 per cent per annum.

The complainant, Krishan Lal, a resident of Sector 20, stated that teeth implanted by the dentist were causing pain in his gums.

Dr Verma had advised Lal to get new teeth implants for which the complainant paid Rs 5,000 as advance. Later, he paid the balance amount of Rs 10,750.

According to the complaint, Lal repeatedly complained of uneasiness and pain in his gums to Dr Verma.

But the dentist assured him that the teeth will adjust in the jaw after some time.

When the problem persisted, Dr Verma told him that the only remedy was to extract the implanted teeth, which Lal did not agree with.

The complainant alleged that the dentist is not a qualified doctor and is misleading patients.

Clarifying his stand, Dr Verma said he is a qualified doctor and registered with the Punjab Dental Council.

He submitted that, in fact, the complainant never underwent treatment at the clinic.

"Lal visited me once and obtained an estimate for the treatment cost, which amounted to Rs 15,750. He did not visit the clinic thereafter. He is misusing that written estimate as evidence," stated the dentist.

Heading: MC regularises hotels at rates nine times less than conversion fee - Indian Express
Content:
In the backdrop of his expulsion from the House, former CM Amarinder Singh today said the files pertaining to the 87 acres exempted by CM Parkash Singh Badal during his previous tenure have gone "missing".

Demanding that the CM should come clean on the issue, Amarinder said the information on the missing files has come by way of an RTI filed by an individual. Addressing newspersons, he said, "The 87 acres were given to three builders by Badal. The official reply from the government is that the file is not traceable."

* Land deals: Amarinder Singh said the Badal government was selling government land, and the money thus colleted was not going to the treasury. Instead, it was being spent on other purposes through Infrastructure Development Boards. "Badal has no authority to do this. Let him sell his own land," he said. So far, assets worth Rs 3,200 crore have being sold, he added.

* Patiala passion: Amarinder said the money that Badal was of late spending "generously" in Patiala was out of the Rs 82 crore he had got for the Patiala Infrastructure Development Board. "I hope Badal spends the money-- as the election to the segment has been put off-- and not take Patiala residents for a ride," he said.

* On Orbit: He said Orbit had 40 buses when Badal came to power. Today, it has a fleet of 100. Buses of even ex-servicemen and handicapped in the Malwa belt have being bought by Orbit, he alleged.

* Haryana SGPC: Amarinder said if the Sikhs want a separate SGPC, why should it be a problem with Badal? It is for the Sikhs of Haryana to decide on this, he said.

* Sonrise: Reacting on the prospects of his son Raninder Singh contesting from Bathinda against the CM's son, Sukhbir Badal, Amarinder said party high command would decide on this.

* Undaunted: Amarinder said he was not afraid of the plans of the Badals to book him in false cases and restrict his movement. "They believe in might is right policy. My life will not be run by the Badals. We will fight them and defeat them. They should fight me and not the Congress workers in Punjab." He said the Congress was filing a case with the ECI for declaring Punjab a sensitive state that should have Central forces during elections.

* Subsidy: Supporting subsidies, Amarinder said it was the duty of the state to look after its 74 per cent small and marginal farmers.

* On Nano: "Punjab offered Tata all they wanted, including 700 acres of land, housing project worth Rs 300 crore and VAT rebate. Despite this and a much-favorable response from Ratan Tata, they went to West Bengal," he said.

* On Bir Devinder and Bhattal: Capt said he and Bhattal were the best of friends. On Bir, he said, "There are two Badals and a Bir Devinder now. The PPCC is handling his case," he said.

Heading: Dalits allege social boycott... - Indian Express
Content:
The UT Municipal Corporation has apparently devised a new way to regularise unauthorised hotels and guesthouses, which flourish in the villages around the city's periphery — allow owners to pay conversion fee nine times less than the prevailing rate.

While three such hotel sites have already been passed by the Municipal Corporation, around 34 approvals are in the pipeline.

Difference

In Chandigarh, Rs 1,000 per square foot is the conversion rate for the first floor and Rs 800 per square foot for the second floor as fixed by the Administration. But the MC apparently follows a different set of rules. Rs 1,300 per square yard (there are nine square feet in one square yard) is what it takes to turn an illegal hotel or guesthouse site into a commercial business. Also, the MC has not adopted any floor-wise conversion policy in the villages as followed in the commercial areas of the city.

The explanation

Justifying the move, MC officials cite the disparity in infrastructure between the planned parts of the city and the villages.

Town Planner M L Arora said: "Yes, the conversion fee for guesthouses and hotels is approximately nine times lesser in the villages than in other parts of the city, but the rates were passed in an MC House meeting. In fact, a committee was constituted to deliberate on the issue and the proposal was approved after it submitted its report."

Mayor Pardeep Chhabra admitted that the conversion rates for guesthouses in the villages are less. "The city hotels earn much more than these guesthouses can hope to earn. In case the by-laws are violated, action will be taken against the offenders."

Flourishing hotels

Newsline found around 250 such unauthorised guesthouses flourishing in the villages. While the room-tariff is the same or higher than the authorised hotels, the facilities provided are much below par. Some are located in narrow alleys, with not enough clear passage for vehicles to reach the front desk. But illegal guesthouses have certainly not compromised on the number of rooms, with most having 15 to 20 rooms.

Yashpal Mahajan, a prominent city-based businessman, said: "The villages should not have such illegal guesthouses or hotels as these are already allowed in the city. What is the need to regularise such shady structures? But as the MC is allowing the conversion, why isn't the same conversion rate applicable there as well?"

"It seems the councillors and MC officials are hand-in-glove with such illegal operators," said another prominent city-based businessman.

Heading: Revenge: ‘KCF terrorist’s main target was Mahesh Inder’ - Indian Express
Content:
...later patch up with Jats

Allegations over social boycott of Dalits and an eventual patch-up kept the village tense all through the day.

Members of the Balmiki community in this village today alleged that the Jat community socially boycotted them following an incident that took place on Sunday, when a gurdwara granthi was beaten up by a Dalit mob.

However later, after SP(H) Satinder Singh cajoled both the parties to bury the hatched, they claimed to have reached a compromise.

The Dalits were annoyed over a religious discourse by the granthi in which he allegedly used some objectionable remarks against Lord Balmiki. Though no case was registered for beating up the granthi, who was saved by timely action by police and the civil administration, the police had booked the members of Jat community under the SC/ST Act and attempt to murder for beating up a Dalit, Rajinder Singh.

However, the administration denied social boycott of Dalits. Heavy police force has been deployed to defuse tension. "Dalits were not

allowed to take fodder from the fields of Jats and milkmen have also stopped selling them milk," said Jaswinder Singh, a villager.

"We cannot use STD booths and also cannot get our grains ground at village flour mill," said another Dalit. Karmi, a Dalit woman working under the Pendu Sikhya Vikas Committee (PSVC), alleged that she was expelled from work today morning.

Villagers working in the grain market, including Nikki, Baljit, Taro, Paramjit, Bille, alleged that they were told by the commission agents not to come for work.

Notably on Sunday, over 100 Dalits, led by one Bhulla and former sarpanch Jasbir Kaur, and others entered the gurdwara and dragged the granthi to the courtyard and started beating him up.

They allegedly also took off his turban, which was returned on Monday after the intervention of police and the civil administration. Former sarpanch Malkiat Singh denied any social boycott. He said the villagers were being instigated by the outsiders for political reasons.

Shahkot SDM Jasbir Singh said there was no social boycott and no one has been expelled from jobs.

When asked about Karmi's case, he said he has told PSVC and grain market employees not to resort to such actions. He said after the incident, people were communicating less and things would normalise after sometime.

Meanwhile, Tarsem Peter of the Pendu Mazdoor Union has submitted a memorandum to Deputy Commissioner Jalandhar, demanding an end to "social boycott".

Heading: Lensman booked for stopping train - Indian Express
Content:
He struck a deal to kill Jassi, dera chief in exchange for help to kill CM's cousin

Binder Singh, an alleged Khalistani Commando Force (KCF) terrorist who was arrested by Bathinda police recently, had struck a deal with hardcore terrorist Harjinder Singh alias DC to eliminate Bathinda MLA Harminder Singh Jassi and Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh in lieu of getting assistance to assassinate Congress leader Mahesh Inder Singh Badal, cousin of Punjab Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal. He had a grudge against Mahesh Inder.

This was claimed by Lambi SHO Harinder Singh, who interrogated Binder today. "During interrogation, Binder alleged that false cases were slapped on him at the behest of Mahesh Inder Singh Badal and he wanted to take revenge," said Harinder.

However, Mahesh Inder said, "I am not comfortable talking about it. Police officials can tell you better. I came to know of the arrest today through newspapers." He denied that a case was registered against Binder at his behest.

Binder has a long criminal record. He was booked for a murder in 1996 and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1999. As per the police, Binder appealed in the higher court and got bail. Three cases of attempt to murder, latest on August 23 at Lambi police station, were registered against him from 2002 to 2008.

He was acquitted in one such case registered in 2003. As per Muktsar SSP GS Gill, Binder also faced cases under the Arms Act and the NDPS Act in 2003, but was acquitted.

A case at Muktsar city police station was also registered against him for escaping from police custody during a court hearing.

Well-placed sources in the police department said even as Binder had criminal cases against him in the past, he had a tryst with terrorism in Ferozepur jail, where he met DC.

Meanwhile, Bathinda district police chose to remain tightlipped. "Binder was wanted by the Muktsar police. He is with them," said Bathinda SSP Ashish Chaudhry and refused to divulge anything about the interrogation of Binder in Bathinda.

Ranjit Singh, CIA in-charge, who reportedly led the police party to arrest Binder, when asked about the location and timing of arrest, said, "I am ill. I do not remember anything."

Jalandhar SSP PK Rai, when asked about the "mysterious escape" of Binder from the custody of the Jalandhar police, said, "He was never arrested by the Jalandhar police. Interrogation of DC revealed about the intentions of Binder. We alerted Bathinda police and provided whatever information and leads we had about Binder."

Heading: Old bags may trigger new trouble - Indian Express
Content:
The photojournalist with a vernacular daily and some of his associates, who had complained against Saif Ali Khan, are in trouble. The Railway Protection Force has registered a case against them for stopping a train at Patiala railway station on September 29.

No arrests have been made so far, as the RPF is awaiting orders from senior officials. An FIR has been registered against Pawan Kumar and others under section 174 of the Railway Act, but cops were earlier treading cautiously and wanted the controversy to be over before they could arrest the accused.

Notably, on September 28, crew members of Saif's production house allegedly thrashed a photographer. The matter was later resolved when Saif tendered an apology, but before that some people stopped the Dadar Express.

In charge of Patiala RPF Dhanna Singh said, "We will arrest the accused on getting orders from seniors."

Heading: Kidderpore 25 Pally spreads tiger conservation message - Indian Express
Content:
Department Food and Civil Supplies asks procurement agencies to use 50 per cent of the old gunny bags used during the wheat season

A recent order by the Department Food and Civil Supplies is likely to cause bitterness between the farmers' union and the procurement agencies.

The department has asked the procurement agencies to use 50 per cent of the old gunny bags this season. Notably, the bags used during the wheat procurement were below the standards set by the government. As highlighted by The Indian Express on April 30, the gunny bags that made way into the mandis weighed 500 grams as against the standard weight of 655 grams. This means, a farmer was not being paid a single penny for 155 grams of wheat.

The loss to the farmers which was about Rs 2 crore for wheat would be much more this time, as against the 90 lakh metric tonnes of wheat procured in Punjab, the figure for paddy is around 144 lakh metric tonnes. Simple calculations show that as paddy is packed in a 35-kilogram gunny bag, a farmer stands to lose Rs 40 for each tonne.

"I have asked farmers to weigh the gunny bags before they sell their crop," said Ajmer Singh Lakhowal, chairman of the Punjab Mandi Board.

"We will sell by the actual weight. I don't want the farmers to lose money," he added. "Procurement will pick up in a day or two and our teams will personally weigh the bags. The procuring agencies will be challaned in case of any discrepancy," he said.

Meanwhile, Director, Food and Civil Supplies, SP Singh said, "These are the orders from the Government of India. We are not forcing the agencies to use the old bags. They have a choice to use new ones."

However, shortage of gunny bags has always been a problem for the procurement agencies. A senior FCI official said, "The bags should be as per the guidelines laid down by the Director of Quality and Assurance, Kolkata, which has the provision for recalling bags which fall short of these specifications. However still, each year, old bags come in circulation."

Heading: No joyride on giant wheel this Puja - Indian Express
Content:
A gradually melting Arctic Circle and the progressively widening aperture in the ozone layer might always be taking a backseat in our minds, but signs of depleting environmental health and disturbed ecological balance closer home rarely fail to grab our attention.

One such issue, which is widely read and discussed, is tigers leaving their natural habitat and finding themselves amid scared and hostile villagers.

"We glance through such news often, ascertain if somebody's hurt or dead, and forget about it altogether," said Shakuntala Bhattacharya, spokesperson of Kidderpore 25 Pally Puja committee.

The organisers, therefore, have decided to base this year's Puja on tiger conservation. "We have to understand why tigers leave the forests and enter villages. This is because of shortage of food," explained Bhattacharya.

The encroachment of forests by humans and a growing population results in the decrease of prey for the animals. "Humans too hunt for deer, boars, which are sources of food for tigers. This leads to a shortage of food for them. So, tigers enter villages in search of food. We all know how they are attacked and are usually injured grievously in such misadventures," said Bhattacharya.

In order to make people aware of the plight of tigers, the organisers have done up their pandal in colours of the beast. Flaming yellow, canary yellow, black and white —- the colours that define a Royal Bengal Tiger, have been used prominently in the pandal.

The aisle that leads to the idol and the pillars alongside are done up with thin panels of wood coloured to resemble tiger skin. The open area along the aisle is boldly done up with giant cane structures that resemble the stripes on the body of a tiger. The structures are placed very close to each other creating an illusion of a giant tiger skin in bold strokes of yellow, black and white. "This is meant to protest against poaching," added Bhattacharya.

The committee has also roped in artistes from Orissa, who will be performing their traditional animal mask dance. The team will be performing under the supervision of Narayan Maharana, who has performed in many countries.

"This is the dance we usually dedicate to the Thakurani mata, where we dress up as animals and parade before her idol, trying to convey that we are at peace with Nature," said Maharana. For the Kidderpore Puja, Maharana has got ten boys to be painted in the colours of a tiger.

"We use water colour but do not mix it with water while applying it on the body. It takes a long time to take it off," said Maharana.

The process is quite painstaking — the boys hold on to bamboos and stretch their arms and legs and stand for nearly an hour before performances for the paint to dry up, said Maharana.

Heading: South Indian palace recreated on south Kolkata street - Indian Express
Content:
The Kolkata police have slapped a ban on all electric giant wheels after one person died and two others were injured in two separate accidents on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"We have asked the Kolkata Municipal Corporation to keep a watch and we have banned electric giant wheels during Durga Puja to prevent such accidents," said Vineet Goyel, Deputy Commissioner (Headquarters), Kolkata police.

On Tuesday night, Dipak Ghosh (65) died of heart attack while taking a joyride on a giant wheel with his grandson at Harish Park in Bhowanipore.

Ghosh was a resident of Roopchand Mukherjee Lane.

The Puja revelry at Deshapriya Park Puja fairground was marred by an accident, in which, two youths fell down from a giant wheel.

The injured were immediately rushed to the AMRI Hospital where they are still recuperating from their injuries.

Heading: Thousands throng pandals to offer anjali - Indian Express
Content:
A south Indian palace standing tall in the middle of a south Kolkata locality can only be thought of during the five days of Durga Puja. After all, it is the only time when one can possibly visit different places without moving out of the city periphery.

This year, Tridhara Sammilani's creation of the Padmanabhapuram Palace on Rash Behari Avenue would provide the pandal-hoppers a mystical illusion of having stepped into the palace in Tamil Nadu.

The only palace in the country to have been made entirely out of wood, the Padmanabhapuram Palace is located at the Padmanabhapuram Fort in the Kanyakumari district. It was constructed in 1601 by Iravipillai Iravivaram Kulasekhara.

Debashish Kumar, secretary of the organising committee said the main idea behind the pandal is to familiarise the people of West Bengal with the historic palace.

The pandal has exquisite woodcarvings. While the original palace is huge, the organisers decided to replicate just the king's chamber for the pandal. "While it took three months to make the wood carvings with 10 artisans working exclusively on them, the entire pandal took six months for completion," Kumar said . "The cost incurred was nearly 12 lakh to get everything made," he added.

What sets this puja apart from the rest is the fact that not just the pandal, but even the idol is a departure from the traditional ones in Bengal. Made out of bronze, the idol is a splitting image of the goddess as would be present in the original palace.

The goddess is not depicted as slaying the asura, but the buffalo, which is considered to be the vehicle of asura. "The asura in this case is symbolic and by slaying the buffalo, the Goddess has slain the asura," said Kumar.

At 6.30 every evening, five priests chant the name of the Goddess 1008 times for an hour and fifteen minutes, as is done in the traditional temples of the south. The different names of Durga are chanted to the beats of the dhak to evoke a sense of fervour. "People troop in the evening just to hear them chant the names. The chants and the dhak make the atmosphere electrical,"Kumar said.

Heading: RTI: officials fined for withholding information - Indian Express
Content:
With mahashtami being the most awaited day during Durga Puja, the city saw thousands of people thronging Puja pandals as early as 9 am on Tuesday.

Mahashtami, the third day of Puja, is considered to be the culminating point of the four-day celebrations. "Today goddess Durga is worshipped as the symbol of power. Besides, a lot of rituals take place on this day. I have been up since the morning to offer anjali to the goddess," said Shaoli Burman, a college student.

As the city pandals were reverberating with mantras, devotees from all over the state were seen queuing up at Belur Math and Ramakrishna Kumari Math at Kamarkundu, which are two of the most popular places in the city where Kumari Puja, a unique ritual of mahashtami, takes place. According to Hindu mythology, it was on this day that goddess Durga, an epitome of supreme beauty and power, had killed powerful demon Mahishasura.

Although mahashtami is marked by a ritual of animal sacrifice, now animals are substituted with chalkumro, cucumber and banana.

Another distinctive feature of the third day of Puja in the state is the ritual of Sandhi Puja, which marks the sandhikkhan, the juncture between mahashtami and mahanabami. In Hindu mythology on this day Durga took the form of goddess Chamunda to kill Mahishasura. "Mahashtami Puja is the most important festival of Bengalis. Every Kolkatan wakes up early and prepares for a host of traditional customs before breaking the fast," said Paroma Sarkar, a housewife.

According to Puja organisers, Mahashtami Puja draws the largest number of devotes to pandals as compared to the other days of the festival.

"Since morning, we have been receiving nearly 3,000 visitors per hour. To perform the Sandhi Puja, people will keep coming the whole night. There is a 30 per cent increase in the footfall today," said D Bhattacharya, committee member of Kumartuli Sarbojanin Durgotsav.

Heading: Forget Singur, industry marches on in Bengal - Indian Express
Content:
More and more Left Front babus are finding the Right to Information (RTI) Act difficult to deal, as they are being fined for stonewalling requests from the rural poor regarding information related to their quota of work and housing under two flagship schemes of the UPA government.

In the latest instance, a block development officer (BDO) was fined Rs 25,000 and a panchayat secretary Rs 20,000, in two separate cases. The only thing common in both the cases was that the officials had refused to part with the information sought.

In the BDO's case, the West Bengal Information Commission (WBIC) had to call in the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of the West Bengal police to track down what turned out to be a forged signature.

In June 2007, one Kartick Rajoar of village Neguira, under Purulia's Puncha block, filed an RTI application with the BDO, Soumen Pal, asking as to why he had not been paid for the four days' of work. He also asked for the muster roll of the entire Chaitu Bandh scheme for January 2007.

Rajoar waited two months for a reply before filing an appeal with the appellate authority, the sub-divisional officer (SDO), on August 13, 2007. After he did not receive any response, Rajoar filed a second appeal with the WBIC on October 23, 2007.

When the commission asked the BDO and the SDO to show cause as to why no action was taken on Rajoar's request, the BDO claimed that Rajoar had received an official reply within ten days of his request, saying he had been paid the wages, and that he should submit the fee required to get a copy of the muster roll.

The WBIC passed on this information to Rajoar, who then told the commission that he had received no such information from the BDO. The WBIC called both the parties to a hearing on June 24, 2008, where the BDO produced the original office copy of the reply purportedly given to Rajoar, signed as received by Rajoar.

Rajoar, after studying the copy, said the signature was not his and that the whole memo had been fabricated by the official.

The WBIC had to ask the CID to probe the matter. It was later found that Rajoar's signature had been forged.

Taking a serious view of the matter, the WBIC imposed a fine of Rs 25,000, the maximum allowed under the Act, on the BDO, to be deducted in five monthly installments from his pay.

The BDO also claimed the letter had been received and signed by Rajoar's daughter. Even this was found to be false. "The malafide intentions of the BDO is further evident due to the fact that he has not mentioned of this fact during the course of hearing or during the explanation submitted by him," the WBIC observed.

In the other case, a panchayat secretary of Hensla gram panchayat, under Arsha block in Purulia district, faced the wrath of the WBIC and a hefty fine for stonewalling requests for information from two villagers, Sunil Kumar Sahish and Gopal Mahato.

On September 13, 2007, in a joint request for information, Sahish had asked for the muster roll of one scheme under the NREGS, while Mahato wanted the complete list of beneficiaries under the Indira Awas Yojana. The panchayat office didn't reply within the stipulated time of 30 calendar days and Sahish and Mahato filed an appeal with the BDO.

Though the BDO is not the appellate authority for gram Panchayats, he ordered that the secretary pass on the information by November 21, 2007.

Sahish and Mahato then paid the fee specified for the information they had sought. When nothing happened, they moved the WBIC, which asked the panchayat secretary to show cause for the delay. The secretary claimed in his reply that the two had not come to collect the information, to which the commission said on April 28, 2008, that the panchayat should send the information by post.

After another wait, the appellants complained once again on June 19 that they had not received any reply.

The WBIC scheduled a hearing with both parties on July 24, at which the secretary said the pradhan had told him on January 3, 2008, that no information should be furnished to any body in the pradhan's absence. The secretary, however, failed to explain his silence from September 13, 2007 (the day he had received the application) to January 3, 2008.

The WBIC noted that information should have been furnished within 30 days but the secretary allowed a delay of 80 days, so he should pay a penalty at Rs 250 per day for 80 days, to be paid in four installments.

Heading: Far from the Madding Crowd - Indian Express
Content:
These days, the probasi Bengali does not fret if he cannot be in Kolkata for puja. Neither does he necessarily want to. While the zealous charm of visiting a puja pandal down every block can only be experienced in Bengal, Bengalis in different part of the world celebrate Maa Durga's homecoming in their own distinctive styles. A probasi Bengali tells us what puja means in his/her corner of the world

I leave my sandals out side and enter the hall. It's been bitter cold for the last few days. I hang up my trenchcoat brushing the raindrops from it and adjust my saree underneath. Its been almost 8 months since I last wore a saree. It's a blessing after the endless succession of drab colored pant-suits. I take in a deep breath and I go back in my mind to the pujas pandal days of Kolkata with the mingled smell of dhoop, dhuno and the beat of the dhak. It feels like home again as I enter the premises of the congregation hall turned into a pujo mondop. Inside is a happy mix of what I would expect to see in any parar puja in Kolkata with a dash of something American thrown in. The flower garlands on the Durga protima are a mix of Indian and American flowers as well as the fruit offerings at Devi Durga's feet. There is the familiar throng of mashima's sitting near the idol, cutting fruit and a few kids running around with sweatshirts pulled over their Indian finery.

The Puja in Queens, New York, isn't much different from that in say Mudiali. And having grown up in a township where Puja meant meeting up with all my friends and having long adda sessions through the day, I still crave that atmosphere. Its fun to see some of the multi cultural Bengali families coming in with either their American jamai decked out in full dhuti-punjabi and very conscious of the freely flowing garment around the lower half of his body or the American bouma looking lovely with a big red tip on her forehead and trying not step on her saree while tugging her aanchol into the right position.

Soon its time for khichuri bhog and tables are laid out. We relish our khichuri and papad and chatni, my friend's american husband has a hard time coping with the food without the aid of forks or spoons but soon gets the hang of it. One mesho-moshai complains loudly that we should have kept aside enough money to get dhakis from Kolkata instead of the recorded 'thing' coming out of someone's iPod.

We stay back for a little bit more to talk to some of our friends, talking about what has been going on in epar Bangla and opar Bangla. And soon its time to leave, it's been a pleasant evening but tomorrow is a work day which means everyone need to head home soon. So puja still holds the same spot in my life, a time to meet up with friends and neighbours I have not seen in ages, catching up on each others stories and celebrating bangaliana in as grand a style as possible.

Heading: 10 of a family die in Burdwan accident - Indian Express
Content:
Rita Ganguly remembers Begum Akhtar not only as ghazal legend but also as a successful woman of the early 20th century

Rita Ganguly sits gracefully in spite of the heat when we meet at the Terrace Café at Triveni Kala Sangam. Further, she shows no sign of hurrying up our chat for her afternoon flight to Mumbai, for the launch of her book on Begum Akhtar. When I ask for her favourite Akhtar anecdote, she laughs: "There are so many stories about Ammi. But what I remember most is one night in 1966 when she went over to my guru and thumri legend Siddheshwari Devi, ending their 32-year-old feud, and asked her for a favour — to let me join her as a disciple." Ganguly is arguably Akhtar's last chosen disciple and after years of hearing many stories about her teacher, she is determined to set the record straight.

Ae Mohabbat: Reminiscing Begum Akhtar (Stellar Publishers, Rs 695) delves into the life and times of Akhtaribai Faizabadi, better known as Begum Akthar. Ganguly writes about an enthusiastic young singer from north India who burst into the scene in the late 1920s and soon became the darling of the music world. "She juggled her multiple roles as a performer, lover, wife, mother, guru and friend," says Ganguly. "But beneath the facade of fame, she was a deeply sensitive woman, facing loneliness, pain and anguish," she adds solemnly.

Ganguly began her research into Akhtar's life in 2000, when, on a Ford Foundation Fellowship, she documented the lives of tawaifs as a musical community, searching for a comprehensive repertoire of their music and, finally, recording over 200 hours of rare music. "Ammi has mistakenly been branded as a tawaif and a thief for decades now. In music circles, women have always been mistreated, misinterpreted. I wanted to write the story of her life from the perspective of a successful, working woman, much ahead of her times," says Ganguly, who in 2002, wrote and performed a solo play called Begum Akhtar and toured extensively with it. The book is as much about Akthar as it is about the emergence of classical music in post-Independence India.

Ganguly's sure that quite a few feathers will be ruffled, "So many of her disciples even claim that I wasn't her student. That's all right. It only lessens the burden of her legacy and allows me to record in whatever genre I want," chuckles Ganguly, who is releasing a thumri album later this month. "Ammi's greatest lesson to me was life, and how to look at it. She used to say, if you want to achieve anything in life, then make friends with loneliness, it won't betray you."

Heading: Ganguly’s daughter gets kidnap threat - Indian Express
Content:
Ten members of a family, including four children, were killed in an accident in Burdwan, about 87 kilometres from Kolkata, on Monday night. The incident took place when the Tata Sumo, in which the family was returning home after visiting pandals, fell into a canal.

Fire Brigade personnel were rushed in from Burdwan and a team of divers was called from Madhyamgram in North 24-Parganas. But it was too late by the time they reached the spot, the members of the family had drowned by then.

The deceased have been identified as Uttam Rakshit (45), his wife Tapati (35) and their two children Soumyo (8) and Ananya (15). Uttam's brother Asim (36), his wife Bidyutlata (32), their children Shilpika (8) and Rittika (5), a nephew Arindam (25) and a sister-in-law Ruma (32), too, died in the accident.

"All of them had planned to go see pandals on Saptami many days ago and the children were very excited about the trip," said Swapan Rakshit, elder brother of Uttam and Asim.

According to police, the families first went to Memari and then to Jamalpur to see idols. They were returning home and were about a kilometer from their village when the tragedy struck at around 11:30 pm.

"The driver of the Tata Sumo failed to negotiate a turn on the approach road to a small bridge over a local canal," said R Rajshekharan, Superintendent of Police, Burdwan. The vehicle broke the brick wall by the side of the road, and fell into the canal. The driver managed to jump out of the vehicle, but none of the ten members who were inside the vehicle could come out, added Rajshekharan.

The driver, who was also injured in the accident, managed to reach the village and informed the villagers about the accident. They rushed to the spot but could not do much due to darkness. The police and the fire brigade were also informed. Three fire engines reached the village around 4 am. But the villagers had already fished out the vehicle from the canal.

"Initially, three bodies, including that of two children, were found in the vehicle," police said. The locals, along with the police, later found the rest of the bodies which had been washed a few hundred feet away in the canal. The last body was found at around 11 am on Tuesday.

Following the death of the family members, the villagers have called off all celebrations. "We have decided not to celebrate Pujas. This day will haunt us every year. No one will be able to forget this dreadful Saptami," said a villager.

Heading: Pushed to the brink, Dada throws off gloves - Indian Express
Content:
On a day when he announced his retirement, Sourav Ganguly has a major worry - a kidnap threat to his daughter. While the cricketer called a press meet in Bangalore to announce his retirement, he admitted that last weekend his family in Kolkata received an anonymous letter, which said that his six-year-old daughter, Saana, could soon be kidnapped.

He added, "it would be better if we don't discuss it (the kidnap threat) here." Sources said the letter also mentioned a ransom amount of Rs 2 crore.

Although it is not yet known if the Ganguly family, which stays in their traditional Behala house, has approached the police, both the relatives and the police have denied that any complaint was lodged in the matter. Ganguly's elder brother Snehasish admitted that the letter had reached them. "Yes, there was a threat letter. We (family members) have discussed the matter and we do not think that the matter is alarming. We are not approaching the police," said Snehasish.

Kolkata's Detective Department chief Jawed Shamim said: "I don't have any knowledge of such a letter. The Kolkata Police are not conducting any investigation in the case either." SP (South 24 Parganas) Ajay Ranade said, "I don't have any information about the letter."

Dona and her father Sanjib Ray also refused to comment.

The letter is learnt to be written in Bengali and was sent to Ganguly's Biren Roy Road residence in Behala through speed post. It is speculated that the letter could have been posted from the Esplanade post office last Friday and it was delivered to the Gangulys on Saturday.

Heading: With Nano in Gujarat, Singur tries to fill vacuum - Indian Express
Content:
Hours before the city was gearing up to celebrate mahashtami on Tuesday, a statement made far away in Bangalore left Kolkata's sports enthusiasts stunned. Amid the sepculations about a 'deal' or a 'golden handshake' forged between him and the Board of Cricket Control of India (BCCI) to facilitate his retirement, Saurav Ganguly said: "I will play in the first two Tests (he was picked for the opening two matches against Australia). After the Australia series, I will retire." The announcement has come just two days before the first India-Australia Test gets underway in Bangalore. Ganguly's decision to quit means it will be curtains for West Bengal cricket's presence at the highest level. Ever since his debut in 1996 with a telling ton at Lord's, Ganguly emerged as India's most successful captain, besides earning the tag of Indian cricket's bad boy, getting embroiled in numerous controversies.

His retirement isn't exactly much of a surprise for those who have been closely following the developments in Indian cricket. Nearly a week ago, when Ganguly was picked for the first two Tests against Australia, speculations were rife that the Indian cricket board had worked out a 'deal' with him. "We are selecting you for these Tests provided you promise us that you will retire after the series and announce it beforehand " - this was the tone of the BCCI message to Ganguly, as The Indian Express had first reported.

Former Bengal stalwart Gopal Bose, manager of the Under-19 Indian team, has played a pivotal role in Ganguly's career on the technical front.

"It's crystal clear that a golden handshake has been worked out. The cricket Board hasn't given him any choice and he has been pushed out of the scene," he said.

Ranji Trophy-winning captain Sambaran Banerjee, who was the national selector when Ganguly made his Test debut, reckons he couldn't have timed this announcement better. "He is the most successful captain of India. He has nothing more to achieve. He has chosen the right time to call it quits. We should hail his decision to retire," Banerjee said .

Ganguly's elder brother Snehasish, also a famous Ranji Trophy batsman, said, "It's not a surprise for the family. He had discussed it with us before. I knew that he would announce his retirement any day now," he said.

State Urban Minister Ashok Bhattacharya, very close to the Ganguly family, said he had prior knowledge of the announcement. "I knew about it. A few days before leaving for Bangalore, he had visited my home and said that he had decided to quit," he said.

Heading: Too few of us to handle terror: Cops - Indian Express
Content:
Just days before the Pujas, the news that Tata is relocating its small car project to Gujarat has come as a rude shock to the people of Singur. It has not only affected the image of the town, its residents have also lost their jobs.

Many of them had hoped that despite Tata Sons' chairman Ratan Tata's announcement to shift the project, the company might change its decision. But with the joint announcement made by Tata and Gujarat Chief Minister Narendra Modi about relocating the project to Gujarat, all hopes have been dashed. Those who thought of earning a livelihood from the project seem demoralised.

"I was hopeful that I would support my family with the job provided by the Tatas. But now I do not know what to do," said Asim Ruidas, a youth of Beraberi Madhyapara. He had taken an apprenticeship course organised by the West Bengal Industrial Development Board and the Tatas.

His brother Akul said: "We had hoped the Tatas might come back later and resume the project. But now, since the factory is being shifted to Gujarat, all hopes are lost."

Manas Khatua, who runs a small tea stall at the main gate of the factory premises, is also clueless. "I had invested my entire savings in setting up this shop. I thought that the stall would do well and I would later expand it. My main customers were Tata employees. I have lost my clients," he said.

The unwilling farmers are also demoralised. Many admitted that this was not what they wanted.

"We had hoped that if we got our land back, we would either resume farming or sell it off at a good price," said a farmer.

The local CPM has not lost all hopes though. Dibakar Das, a local CPM leader, said: "We know that the Nano project has been shifted. But Tatas never said they would not build any industry here. We will request the government to persuade the Tatas to set up some other industry here."

Residents are, however, not so optimistic. Sheikh Jiarul, a resident of Joymollah village who willingly gave his land for the project, said: " Some people are saying that the Tatas might set up something else here. But I think that the Tatas have gone forever, at least as far as Singur is concerned."

The local youths, who supplied building materials and other minor items to the factory and the ancillary units, carried out a procession in Singur market on Tuesday. They sat on a dharna outside the Tata factory's gate and decided to approach the Governor and the Prime Minister to intervene in the Singur issue. "We want the Tatas to come back. We will appeal to them," said Raju Mal, a youth.

Heading: Peerbhoy bowled over by hacking course - Indian Express
Content:
15 arrests, all by forces from outside city. Pune police cite lack of inputs and personnel

Since July, when Bangalore and then other cities were hit by chain after chain of blasts, Pune has seen the arrest of 15 SIMI and Indian Mujahideen (IM) members, some residents of Pune, the rest visiting the city on various assignments.

The Pune police, however, seemed unaware of it till the arrests were made. Till the Mumbai crime branch disclosed that the IM had a full-fledged "media wing", an explosive assembly unit and a "control room" at Ashoka Mews apartment complex in Kondhwa, the city police knew nothing of it, though the control room had been in use for a year.

Asked if the Pune police had failed to collect information about the control room, DC (special branch) Ravindra Sengaonkar took the "understaffed" line that the police have been taking whenever anything has gone wrong.

"We have only 7,000 cops against a population of 50 lakh. Information about terror suspects can be collected effectively only if citizens are alert and pass on inputs to the police."

A senior officer from an intelligence agency said that city police stations were negligent about inputs about jehadi movements that they received from sources. "Many times, the police chowky staff neither verified the inputs properly nor did they forward this information to the special branch. It might be because of the load on the local police like heavy bandobast duties and significant growth in routine crimes like thefts, robberies and domestic disputes," the officer said.

State ATS chief Hemant Karkare conceded there was no arrest by Pune police, but said they were working on some inputs. "We have increased surveillance in Pune. We may take help from Pune police whenever needed," he said.

When the Gujarat and Bangalore police and the state Anti Terrorism Squad arrested some key SIMI and IM members with Pune links, the city police had again seemed to have been caught unawares.

In fact, the last time the city police caught any member of SIMI was in 2001. A few SIMI members including local leader Sajid Sundke were arrested in March 2001 for their alleged involvements in communal riots in Ghorpade Peth and Ganj Peth.

This despite the fact that intelligence agencies have always maintained that a jihadi movement in Pune had hit an upward curve with a majority of the activities centred around Kondhwa, Camp, Khadki, Ghorpadi, Ganj Peth and the outskirts of the city.

In 2002, three youths from Pune were arrested in connection with Mulund blasts. Then, in 2003, Anwar Ali, an Urdu scholar working as ad hoc lecturer at the National Defence Academy in Pune was arrested for allegedly providing shelter to LeT and SIMI activists connected to Mulund blasts.

In 2006, Sohail Shaikh of Bhimpura, Pune Camp, a suspected SIMI activist, was arrested in Pune by the state ATS in connected with 7/11 Mumbai local train blasts. Rizwan Davare, the prime suspect in the train blasts was also from Pune.

Investigations revealed that the process of indoctrinating the Pune youths into jihadi culture was on in Pune during this period, even after SIMI was banned in September 2001. But since the March 2001 riots, the Pune police had only 48 names of SIMI suspects on their official record.

The police were jolted out of their inertia when the state ATS unit busted a SIMI module with the arrest of four youths in the city after the Ahmedabad blasts and police commissioner Satyapal Singh ordered the special branch officers to upgrade the list of SIMI suspects in the city. The number of SIMI suspects then went over 300.

Heading: In flats around ‘control room’, murmurs of dubious tenant & suspicious visitors - Indian Express
Content:
Last July, when this 31-year-old software engineer completed a course in ethical hacking and cyber crime, he posted his feedback on the website of the firm that hosted the programme: "Mind boggling,"wrote Mohammed Mansoor Asghar Peerbhoy, or Mannu. "Really unleashes the power of information."

A software architect at the Pune office of the Yahoo! India-owned firm Zimbra, Mansoor attended the six-day course on network security at Internet security solutions firm E2Labs in Banjara Hills, Hyderabad. "It was a one-time crash course on network security, and Mansoor had already done some courses on the subject," said a spokesperson for E2Labs. The course included training in protection of information security, cyber law, phishing, hacking, identity theft and online fraud.

Among the others who attended the course was a computer crime investigator and forensic analyst with the Andhra Pradesh State Forensic Laboratory. Peerbhoy's online feedback, in bullet points, also said: "Very well designed course (obstacle race); very helpful people; very hands on."

A senior officer of the Mumbai Police Crime Branch confirmed that this was being investigated.

Peerbhoy's brother Adil, who works as an architect, told The Indian Express, "We came to know about the allegations against Mansoor only yesterday from the press. We have never heard of any Riyaz Bhatkal or the other names being mentioned. My family is going through a very tough time now. We want to verify details ourselves, only then will we be able to say anything.""

Colleagues at the eSpace IT Park office of Zimbra refused to speak about the man who Mumbai Police have said earned Rs 19 lakh a year, an official spokesperson for Yahoo! India said: "We are very concerned about these events and will fully cooperate with the law enforcement agencies, consistent with local laws."

Zimbra, set up in California and taken over by Yahoo! India last year, offers the Zimbra Collaboration Suite software, a groupware product for messaging and collaboration, emailing, group calendars, web document management, etc. It also provides software to sync mobile devices.

The Mumbai Police have said Peerbhoy, an extraordinarily talented software developer and resident of Pune and belonging to a "highly educated family", travelled several times to the United States on work.

Russian engineer Igor Sysoev, whose opensource software nginx is used by Zimbra, said in an emailed response to The Indian Express: "I know Mansoor as Zimbra developer because Zimbra software uses my opensource software nginx mail proxy server. However, I do not know him personally and until now I do not even know his religious commitment."

(With inputs from Mustafa Plumber)

Heading: Road that caused all the suffering will be ready... after the event - Indian Express
Content:
The man who owns the flat dubbed the Indian Mujahideen's "control room" is ailing. The man who rented it seems to have vanished.

Residents of Ashoka Mews apartment complex in upmarket Kondhwa said they had always had doubts about the tenant. On Tuesday they appointed a spokesman, S S Mirza, who said, "Ten months ago a resident complained that some suspicious youths, instead of the tenant's family, were living in flat H-302."

That is the flat where the control room is said to have thrived. It is owned by Reza Naba, who lives in Pune Camp and let it out to Dr Anwar Bagwan.

"Reza rented out his flat about a year and a half ago. Our rules don't allow bachelors to stay as tenants; Reza told us that Bagwan was married and the agreement too says so, but we never saw his wife," Mirza said.

"When a resident complained that some youths and no family were staying in the flat, the society chairman sent for Reza. Reza started an argument, insisting that Bagwan was a family man, that his wife visited the flat on and off. We still have not seen Bagwan's wife, but the matter was never raised," Mirza added.

After the terror bust, Mirza said residents had no idea about the relations between the arrested men Bagwan and Reza. Reza was not available for comment. A person who picked up the call on his mobile phone said, "I am Reza's uncle. He is under medical observation."

The Kondhwa police have a copy of the agreement between Reza and Bagwan. DC (special branch) Ravindra Sengaonkar said, "We are yet to confirm the details mentioned."

Heading: Resurrecting the Mughals - Indian Express
Content:
The special route for the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG) will hardly be used by those for whom it was intended. Only a handful of participants will take the special route from the airport to Balewadi; the rest will travel take the expressway from Mumbai.

A last-minute patch-up job is all the roads are getting, instead of the complete makeover that was originally planned. The patch-up, which is nearly complete, aims only to make the roads usable. The Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) has suspended construction work and is now beautifying the roads.

Nearly 80 per cent of the foreign participants will travel directly from Mumbai to the sports village, organising committee chairman Suresh Kalmadi said. Another official said 25 buses would ferry 2,000 participants from the Mumbai international airport to the sports village. The rest, along with Indian participants, delegates and guests, will use the special route after landing at the Pune airport.

Civic activist Vivek Velankar is aghast, given what citizens had gone through. "After the civic administration made citizens suffer for the roadwork, the foreign participants are taking the expressway. What was the rush all about?" he said. He pointed out that crores had been spent on the roadwork and questioned its quality.

The administration had planned a special route from Pune airport to the sports complex via Bund Garden and Ganeshkhind Road. Work on Airport Road is nearly done but the Baner Road stretch remains although six contractors were appointed to speed up work.

The PMC is tarring a 2-km stretch instead of laying it in concrete. Under criticism for the slow pace of work, the civic administration recently made it clear that the road, the main route from the city to the sports village, would not be redone completely but merely made usable for the Youth Games.

"Baner Road has got a facelift and the 2-kilometre stretch has been tarred for lack of time. It will be laid in concrete after the Games," said city engineer Prashant Waghmare, who is overseeing the work on the road. "The subway crossing the Mumbai-Bangalore highway is complete and will be opened before the Games. Whatever work was possible, we have completed in record time."

"The PMC is racing against time and the civic staff has put in all its efforts. We are ready for the Games and have taken up the last-minute work of beautification," Municipal Commissioner Praveensinh Pardeshi said.

Heading: India at a glance - Indian Express
Content:
Relive the romance of another era with Alpana Gujral's beautiful designs

Alpana Gujral walks into the Sea Lounge at the Taj Mahal Palace and Tower looking like the very embodiment of style. Dressed simply but elegantly in pastel shades and decked out in jewellery of her own design, the renowned jeweller makes a stunning picture, just like her one-of-a-kind pieces. She is showing her latest collection, The Enchanted Garden, at the hotel. Today is the last day of the show.

The line is inspired by the perfection and symmetry of medieval Mughal gardens. "The theme allowed me to play with different forms and colours," she explains, "The flowers, animals, trees - they all go well with the feminine form and add romance to the pieces."

Gujral has a very simple work philosophy, she informs us. "I believe that there should be an emotional connection between the jewellery and the wearer. You should feel pleasure when you wear a piece. It shouldn't just be for its monetary value. In fact, I strongly believe that jewellery should be more than just an investment."

Gujral's designs are certainly more than that. Exquisitely imagined and realised, her work finds its inspiration in jewellery of the Mughal era. "I think the Mughal age was the height of jewellery design in India - the jadau technique, the enamelling at the back. There's a saying about ornaments from that time - the front of the piece is for the visual pleasure of the person standing in front of you and the decoration at the back is for the soul."

The designer believes that accessories have come of age in India. "In the last few years, jewellery as an accessory has become an important part of everyone's attire," she explains, "This is more so, because costume jewellery is widely available, so everyone can now afford to splurge more on them." Do her outfits revolve around jewellery or vice versa? She laughs and says, "I always co ordinate my clothes to match my jewellery, not the other way round." And what is her opinion on India's legendary obsession with gold? "I completely agree that gold is beautiful," she says, "It's such a warm metal and so malleable. It can take any form."

About her working style, Gujral says, there is no method to her madness. "It is very difficult to describe my style. There is no pattern that I follow. I get an idea and I execute it. But there are days when I have a mental block and then it gets very frustrating. But that is all part of the creative process. I've learnt to be patient with it," she smiles.

Heading: Art with heart - Indian Express
Content:
Art director Somnath Lohar is the man behind the eye-catching stage being made for the upcoming CYG that displays an amalgamation of traditions and cultures of all the states of the country

It may be only a small corner in the entire canvas of the mega event- Commonwealth Youth Games, but Lohar, with his creativity and architectural expertise has put on display a stage that one cannot ignore-for in mere one glance it manages to convey the culture and tradition of the entire country.

"I came to know that the organisers of CYG are looking for someone who can portray the culture of India at the venue. I put my design across to the company named Rang Puhar. My design got approved and here I am working for the CYG," smiles Lohar.

Lohar who has been the art director for a number of films like Saawariya, Corporate, Pyaare Mohan, Masti and so on says, "When they told me that the design and the set needs to represent Indian culture, the first thing that came to my mind was that India does not have one fixed culture. The tradition and culture of India as a country are an amalgamation of cultures of individual states. And while putting across the tradition of our country to the outsiders it is of utmost importance that we display this unity in diversity that we keep boasting about."

Thus on a 350 feet by 150 feet stage near the Hockey stadium at Balewadi, Lohar along with his team, is busy erecting a set up that displays the homogeneity in the closely knit cultures of various states. "I have put on display the important aspects of eight states due to the lack of availability of space. For instance Maharashtra has replicas of forts, bullock carts, Maavlas and so on. Kerala is about Kathakali, elephants, Punjab about tractors and wheat farms and so on. I have used cut outs of typical houses in Sikkim to portray Sikkim. Goa comes alive with huge coconut trees, beaches and so on," adds he.

The stage also represents Howrah bridge of Kolkata, Shikaras and Dal Lake from Kashmir, deserts of Rajasthan and so on. "Yes that is the motive. We are working on it for the past 25 days and the work should be complete byl October 10," says the man who's hoping that this small corner remains an unforgettable one in the corner of the visitors' hearts.

Heading: Small Talk - Indian Express
Content:
A part from creating a world-class art, Mystic Village Creative Art Club is also extending financial support to upcoming art students

Pune has often been called the cultural hub of Maharashtra, teeming with citizens who not only promote but also nourish and sustain genuine art as well as artists. Professor Shubhada Ramesh Bhosale has taken one such initiative by creating the Mystic Village Creative Art Club. An artist herself, she felt that while Pune is vibrant in the spheres of education, drama, dance and music, the field of fine arts, such as drawing painting and sculpture was comparatively neglected.

Hence arose the idea of an artists workshop that would be a haven for painters, sculptors and artists over the world to meet, exchange ideas and create art. The Mystic Village Artist Camp is located at Darawali, Paud, a 23-km ride from Pune City . Their latest artists workshop began last week and was open to international artists as well this year. Participating were Evariccoria Berj from Norway, Buddi Thapa from Nepal, Prem Sunyoto and Madhu Sunyoto from Australia. Among the 70 artists were noted artists from Pune such as Murli Lahoti, Raosaheb Gurav, and D S Khatavkar, as well as artists from Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Jammu, Ujjain, Karnataka and Hyderabad. "From Jammu to Banglore and Gujarat to Kolkata, we have covered art across the land," enthuses Professor Bhosale.

While the artists were immersed in their work the entire day, come evening and the fun began! From Brazilian fire dancers to folk song and dance from Dehradun, from a Sarod and Tabla performance to a relaxing evening listening to the senior citizen orchestra, the camp was truly a melting pot of art and culture.

To preserve the peaceful working atmosphere and let the artists work uninhibited, the venue was open to art lovers and art students only on October 5 strictly from 4pm to 6pm. One could wander around the campus, take in the beautiful exhibits and interact with the artists themselves.

This niche field has always had to struggle for survival, hence a part of the proceeds from the sales will be used to support one of their upcoming art students.

Heading: Dance into shape - Indian Express
Content:
Celebrating tradition

Eighth day of Navratri witnessed a huge crowd turning up to participate in Dandiya nights. The event was organised at Yash Lawn. It was fun time for the youth, who, in vibrant chaniya cholis and traditional dresses, had an opportunity to let their hair down and flaunt their dandiya skill. Taking the euphoria to another eight, another dandiya raas with the live orchestra Music India has been scheduled for today evening at 7.30. The event is being jointly organised by Jazzmataz and New Club.

For dance, with love

If you live dance then here is an opportunity to pay homage to the passion of your life. Parimal Phadke pays tribute to dance with his programme kaleidoscope – ode to the past present and future of dance. Phadke will be performing on October 8 at Durga puja samiti, Mhatre bridge

Heading: Health Corner - Indian Express
Content:
With more and more gyms introducing various dance forms, burning calories has become a lot more fun

Striving for fitness in a gym has often been about working hard for hours on the heavy machines. The idea itself refrains a few from getting that perfect shape. However, fitness may not be about machines these days as many of the gymnasiums are seen breaking conventions of formal fitness trainings and introducing newer ways to remain fit.

With dance steps replacing the treadmill walks and songs in place of the counts, dance remains the new mantras to get in shape.

Be it belly dancing, Latin dances or even Bollywood dances, men and women are definitely more enthusiastic on hitting the gym.

Shirley Singh, a dance instructor in Abs gym, has been innovative about the exercise routines in the fitness center. "I include dances that are fun and at times based on a theme. Its dandiya time and we have been dancing to the dandiya and garba beats. During Holi we have the holi songs. I make sure they perspire and burn those extra calories with this high intensity aerobics. Infact personally I have never done workouts at all, these dances are any time more interesting without realising the efforts. I also teach rock and roll, belly dancing, Bollywood dances and more depending upon the requests from my clients," adds Singh.

Tanaaz Nair, sales head of Gold's Gym says, "A lot of women approached us to introduce dance sessions since the machine routines get monotonous. Most of our customers are 25 plus women and the dances we have are belly dancing and Latin dancing which invariably work on every part of the body especially waist, thighs and stomach and make the whole activity exciting."

The newly launched Tushar Fitness Studio also has a fusion dance in addition to the Latin and Bollywood dances. Speaking on the trend, Rashmi Uttam, director of TFS, says, "We concentrate on the physical as well as mental well-being. Hence for professionals who have a tough day, these power filled exercises act as a stress buster as well as enhance their social skills as far as the dance moves are concerned.

They make a person more expressive, involved and ensure mental wellness simultaneously." Rajesh Arora, instructor at T FS takes his students through the Latin American moves. "Dancing can be as beneficial as cario vascular excercises. I have an amazing response from all age groups," says Arora.

Dr Ruchira Beri has been attending dance classes for the past five months . "I joined the classes just to enjoy, but italso helped me tone my body. It is truly a double bonanza," adds Beri.

Heading: The slug-fest continues - Indian Express
Content:
Infertility Update

Dr Khurd's Infertility, ICSI and Test-Tube Baby Centre organised the Infertility Update-2008 to commemorate its silver jubliee year. Dr Sindhutai Paranjape organised the event, which was chaired by well known gynaecologists of Pune including Dr A Vumranikar, Dr Sulochana Gaikwad and Dr Kapila Bharucha. Dr Rupin Shah, well known andrologist from Mumbai, revealed some facts about infertility. According to Shah, "Human reproduction is intricate and although all secrets about fertility are yet to be unraveled, what we do know is, that husbands contribute towards 50 per cent of the causes of infertility in couples." Male Infertility is coming up with the changing trends of lifestyle. The main reasons being — increasing stress of competition, irregular eating and sleeping habits, obesity and vices like smoking, tobacco, gutkha and alcohol. Talking about the semen analysis, Dr Shah said that this analysis gives important information about sperm counts, their mobility and morphology and regular fluctuations in the counts and mobility is physiological and natural. Many of the laboratories still use old criteria of semen parameters which result in abnormally low or false reports. Besides the oration, many interesting talks were held on topics like assisted reproduction, stem cells, polycystic ovaries and test-tube baby. Dr Sadhana Desia released Apla Bal, a new plan to financially help the infertile couples in treatment. A booklet, Miracles in Infertility, a collection of experiences of doctors helping the infertile couples was also released on the occasion.

Talent contest

On the occasion of the World Mental Health Day, Chaitanya Mental Health Care Centre, a trust that works towards treatment and community rehabilitation of people suffering from chronic mental illness, is organising a talent contest on October 10. The show will be held at Tilak Smarak Mandir, Pune. Aiming at mental heath promotion, education and illness prevention, the trust, has been organising this contest among the residents undergoing treatment in various governmental and non-governmental facilities in the state for the past three years.

Financial help sought

Roshni Salhotra, a 13-year-old girl, suffering from cancer needs chemotherapy followed by surgery. The approximate expenses for her entire treatment would be Rs 2,00,000. Her mother, Mary Angelina is a single mother taking care of two children. The Deenanath Mangeshkar Hospital and Research Centre is taking care of the girl. Your financial help can save the girl.

Arthroscopy meet held

The Indian Arthroscopy Society gathered for their 7th Annual Conference at Goa Medical College to discuss on the issue of 'controversies of arthoscopy' in Goa from September 25 to 27. A panel of experts and delegates debated and discussed the topic and also held lectures and surgical video demonstrations. With a motive to train the younger doctors the Anthroscopic techniques of knee and shoulder, Pune-based doctors, Dr Parag Sancheti, Dr Ashish Babhulkar and Dr Sachin Tapasvi organised conference where Dr Parag Sancheti was elected as Secretary of Indian Anthroscopy Society.

Seminar on injury prevention

With the terrorist activities and bomb blasts increasing, disaster management and prevention of injuries is the need of the hour. Keeping in mind that doctors need to be well equipped to give early treatment during such mishaps, on October 13, the Maharashtra University of Health Sciences has organised a seminar on injury prevention control with special focus on management of bomb blast injuries. Led by Dr Mrudula Phadke, the seminar will have surgeons, orthopedicians, anesthetics and specialists working in hospitals and institutes under MUHS, will talk on various issues. The meet will be held from 1-5 pm at MUHS Regional Centre, 3rd Floor, ESIS Hospital Building, Aundh. The meet is also open to private practitioners. Entry is on first- come-first-serve basis. Interested participants can contact Dr Shere for registrations on 020 27285695 or 9850635000

Conference postponed

The Ayurved and Unani 2008 conference organised by Maharashtra University of Health sciences, regional centre, Pune, has been extended to January 17 and 18 2009, instead of October 4 and 5 2008. This has been done on account of the held up admissions of all Ayurved and Unani colleges of the state to Ayush, the ayurved council of Government of India. The conference will be held at Bal Gandharv Rangmandir, Pune.

Heading: Survey says astrology not a science; astrologers up in arms - Indian Express
Content:
Now, lawyers take it out on policemen

The lawyer-police tiff is turning murkier by the day. A police constable was on Tuesday roughed up and beaten up by the lawyers at the Ashoka Hall of the Shivajinagar district and sessions court. The move was in retaliation to the beating of advocate Rajendra Shinde, said lawyers present in the court premises. The situation become tense as the police armed with sten guns arrived inside the court premises as the news spread.

At a meeting of the lawyers at Ashoka Hall inside the court premises to condemn the way the police treated advocate Shinde, police constable Satish Vir was found recording the proceedings of the meeting. Enraged lawyers got hold of him and beat him up. Even the journalists were not spared as the lawyers roughed up some of them.

Policemen present in the court premises informed police inspector Rahul Kumar Yevle of Shivajinagar Police Station about the situation in the court. When he reached the premises, he too was roughed up by the lawyers. Soon, the police force reached the court premises.

The situation turned ugly after the lawyers asked the police to vacate the court premises. This led to an altercation between the lawyers and the police.

Special judge P R Bora had to intervene to bring the situation under control.
